practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Nicene Creed says about the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points, e.g. (1) The Father is creator of all things; (2) The Son is 'God from God, Light from Light' — one substance with the Father; (3) The Holy Spirit is the Lord and giver of life. Three separate identifiable points required.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about creation.
practice_questions.marks: Responses may include: God created the universe ex nihilo; Genesis 1–3 is the key text; creation is declared 'very good'; God is revealed as benevolent, omnipotent and eternal through the act of creation; humans are created in the image of God. Award marks for three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic teachings about the Incarnation.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations required. E.g. (1) Jesus is fully God and fully human — the eternal Son of God took on human flesh, and this belief is rooted in John 1:14 ('the Word became flesh'); (2) The Incarnation consecrates human life — because God entered human experience, human flesh has profound dignity, and this underpins Catholic care for the sick and vulnerable. Development beyond a bare statement is required for each point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways Catholics understand the relationship between humans and creation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points required, with at least one named source. E.g. (1) Dominion: Genesis 1:28 gives humans authority over the natural world, sometimes interpreted as the right to use creation for human benefit; (2) Stewardship: the modern Catholic reading, reflected in Pope Francis's Laudato Si', sees humans as guardians accountable to God for the care of creation. The 5th mark requires a named source — Genesis 1:28, or a named papal document.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways the doctrine of the Trinity is shown in Matthew 3:13–17.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) The Son (Jesus) is present, being baptised; (2) The Holy Spirit descends as a dove; (3) The Father speaks from heaven, identifying Jesus as his beloved Son.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important Catholic belief is that God is Trinity.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; weighs perspectives explicitly; conclusion justifies a clear position. May argue: FOR — the Trinity is the organising belief of all Catholic theology; every sacrament, prayer and creed is Trinitarian in structure; without it, the Incarnation and salvation have no framework. AGAINST — some argue belief in the oneness of God (shared with Judaism and Islam) is more fundamental; the Incarnation or salvation might be considered more pastorally significant. Named sources: Nicene Creed; John 1:1; Matthew 3:13–17. Secure (7–9): both sides with some development and at least one source. Developing (4–6): one side stronger. Emerging (1–3): minimal, one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about revelation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points, for example: God has revealed himself through the Old Testament prophets; God revealed himself most fully through Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:1-4); God's revelation is ongoing through the Church and scripture; the natural world reflects God's presence and is a form of general revelation. Three distinct points required; elaboration of one point does not earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Outline three details of the miracle recorded in John 4:43-54.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for accurate description: a royal official asked Jesus to heal his son who was near death (1); Jesus told him to go home, that his son would live, without travelling to him (1); when the official checked the timing, his son's recovery began at the exact hour Jesus spoke (1). Full marks require three accurate details.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Catholics believe visions provide evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Visions often result in moral transformation and deepened faith in those who experience them, suggesting they come from a source beyond the human mind (2); The consistency between biblical visions (Genesis 15, Matthew 17) and later visions shows a pattern of divine communication rather than random hallucination (2). Other valid reasoning accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Catholics believe the miracles at Lourdes support belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for first reason with development; 2 marks for second reason with development; 1 mark for a named source of wisdom or authority. For example: The 72 Church-recognised miracles have withstood medical investigation by doctors of all faiths, and no natural explanation has been found, suggesting divine action (2); John 4:43-54 records Jesus performing a miracle at a distance, establishing a precedent that God can act beyond the limits of the natural world, which Catholics see reflected at Lourdes (2); source credit for citing John 4:43-54 or Hebrews 1:1-4 explicitly (1). A paraphrased source without a named reference does not earn the fifth mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Miracles at places like Lourdes are the strongest evidence Catholics have for the existence of God.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; argument weighs perspectives explicitly; conclusion justifies a clear position. May argue Lourdes miracles are strong evidence (72 officially recognised healings, independent medical investigation, John 4:43-54 biblical precedent) but evaluate whether this beats other arguments (cosmological, design, religious experience) or whether atheist rebuttals (Hume, natural explanations) undermine the case. Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present but may not weigh the evidence explicitly. Developing (4-6): One side more developed; sources vague or absent; conclusion descriptive. Emerging (1-3): One-sided; very brief; no named sources. SPaG marks reward correct use of theological vocabulary: miracle, revelation, Lourdes, Transfiguration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which visions have been important in Catholic history, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation); 1 mark for a named source. For example: The Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13) confirmed the disciples' belief in Jesus as the Son of God by revealing his divine glory alongside Moses and Elijah (2); Joan of Arc's visions guided her to support the French king and led to her eventual canonisation in 1920, showing the Church accepts non-biblical visions when they are confirmed by holy living (2); source credit for Matthew 17:1-13 or Genesis 15 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of Allah as taught in the Qur'an.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete characteristics, e.g. (1) Tawhid — Allah is one and indivisible, with no partner or associate; (2) Omnipotence — Allah is all-powerful, the creator of all things; (3) Mercy — Allah is Ar-Rahman (universally merciful) and Ar-Rahim (specifically merciful). Three separately identifiable points.

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Three of the six, each clearly named, e.g. (1) belief in Allah and his oneness; (2) belief in his angels (Malaikah); (3) belief in the Day of Judgement. One mark per distinct belief; no development is needed.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam and the Five Roots of Shi'a Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) The Shi'a Five Roots include Imamah (the leadership of the Imams from the Prophet's family) — this belief is absent from the Sunni Six Beliefs and is the most distinctive Shi'a addition; (2) The Sunni Six Beliefs include al-Qadr (divine decree/predestination) as a separate article; the Shi'a approach this differently through Adl (divine justice), stressing human free will. Development required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about prophethood, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Allah sent prophets to every community — Surah 2:136 names prophets from Abraham to Jesus, confirming that all were sent as guides; (2) Muhammad is the 'seal of the prophets' — the final and greatest prophet, after whom no further prophethood is needed since the Qur'an is complete. 5th mark requires a named source: Surah 2:136 or Surah 16:35–36.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about the holy books (Kutub).
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points: (1) Allah revealed books to his prophets — the Tawrat to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud, the Injil to Isa, the Qur'an to Muhammad; (2) Earlier books became corrupted over time by human error; (3) The Qur'an is the final, uncorrupted revelation of Allah and has supreme authority.

practice_questions.text: 'Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. FOR: Tawhid is the first and foundational belief; shirk (violation of Tawhid) is the only unforgivable sin in Islamic theology; Surah 112 reduces all of Islam to this single truth; every Islamic practice (Salah, Shahada, Hajj) expresses Tawhid. AGAINST: Risalah is equally essential — without prophets and the Qur'an, no Muslim would know how to worship Allah; the Day of Judgement may be more practically motivating for daily Islamic life; Shi'a Muslims might argue Imamah is distinctively important for their community. Named sources: Surah 112; Surah 2:136; Surah 16:35–36. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

practice_questions.text: Outline three attributes of God found in the Mool Mantar (Guru Granth Sahib 1).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three attributes identified and briefly explained. Acceptable: Ik Onkar (God is One — absolute monotheism); Satnaam (God's name is Truth — God is the ultimate reality); Karta Purakh (God is the Creator Being); Nirbhau (without fear); Nirvair (without hatred); Akaal Moorat (beyond time, undying); Ajooni (unborn); Saibhang (self-existent); Gur Prasad (known through the Guru's grace).

practice_questions.text: Outline three Sikh teachings about the purpose of human life.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Human life is a rare and precious opportunity to unite with God (1 mark). Of all living beings, humans have the unique capacity to reflect on the divine and choose the path of liberation (1 mark). Without spiritual practice, the soul remains in the cycle of rebirth (karma and rebirth); liberation (mukti) is the ultimate goal — Guru Granth Sahib 12 describes human birth as a blessing for this purpose (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Sikh beliefs about mukti (liberation from rebirth).
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per belief. Belief 1: mukti is liberation from the cycle of rebirth — when the soul unites with God through God's grace (nadar), the cycle ends; Guru Granth Sahib 78 states that meditating on God's name frees the mortal from rebirth. Belief 2: mukti cannot be achieved through human effort alone but requires God's grace (nadar/kirpa) — even perfect ethical living is insufficient without God turning his grace toward the soul; this distinguishes Sikh understanding from purely merit-based karma systems.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the belief that God's light dwells in all creation shapes Sikh life today.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: because God's light (Jot) is present in every human being, all people have equal worth regardless of caste, gender or religion — this motivates Sikh commitments to equality, sewa (service) and the langar (communal kitchen open to all). Way 2: because creation itself carries God's light, Sikhs are called to treat the natural world with respect and to care for other living beings as expressions of the divine. 5th mark: ‘Guru Granth Sahib 349 tells Sikhs to recognise the Lord's light within all and not to judge people by social class or caste.’

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in mukti is the most important teaching in Sikhism.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: mukti is the ultimate goal of human life — Guru Granth Sahib 2 and 78 make liberation central; without the hope of mukti, Sikh practice (Nam Japna, sewa, kirtan) loses its ultimate purpose; the entire Guru Granth Sahib can be read as a guide to achieving mukti. Arguments against: the Mool Mantar's description of God (GGS 1) is arguably more foundational because it defines who God is — without this, mukti has no object; the three duties (Nam Japna, kirat karni, vand chakna) may matter more as practical guides to daily living than eschatological liberation; equality (GGS 349) and sewa (GGS 26) are central to Sikh identity in contemporary life, arguably more immediately important than abstract liberation. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least GGS 2 or GGS 78 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Sikh and Christian beliefs about the afterlife.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference. Difference 1: Sikhism teaches mukti — the soul merges with God, ending the cycle of rebirth (GGS 78); Christianity teaches resurrection — the body is raised and the individual lives eternally in the presence of God (John 11:25). Difference 2: Sikhism emphasises God's grace (nadar) as the primary means of liberation alongside Nam Japna; Christianity emphasises faith in Jesus Christ as the means of salvation — 'I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me will live' (John 11:25).

practice_questions.text: Outline three Old Testament expectations of the Messiah at the time of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete points, e.g.:
• Many expected a warrior king in the tradition of David who would defeat Rome by force.
• Some hoped for a priestly figure who would restore pure worship in the Temple.
• Others anticipated a prophetic voice, like Elijah, calling the nation to repentance.
• Isaiah 53 describes a suffering servant — though this interpretation was not widely held before Jesus.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events of the baptism of Jesus as recorded in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points, e.g.:
• Jesus came from Galilee to be baptised by John in the River Jordan.
• As Jesus came up from the water, the heavens were 'torn open' and the Holy Spirit descended on him like a dove.
• A voice from heaven declared: 'You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the baptism of Jesus is important for Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per reason: one for a basic point, two for a developed explanation.
• The baptism established Jesus's identity as the Son of God, confirmed by the Father's voice — this gives Christians confidence that Jesus truly was divine, supporting the doctrines of the Trinity and the Incarnation.
• The baptism models the Christian sacrament of baptism — since Jesus submitted to baptism himself, most denominations see it as the rite of initiation into the Church, marking the beginning of a Christian's life of faith.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the title 'Son of Man' helps Christians understand who Jesus is.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point (one for point, one for development), plus one mark for a named source:
• 'Son of Man' connects Jesus to Daniel 7:13, where a heavenly figure is given 'dominion and glory and a kingdom' by God — this shows Jesus as a cosmic figure with divine authority, not just a human teacher.
• Jesus also uses 'Son of Man' when predicting his own suffering and death, showing that the path to glory runs through sacrifice — this shapes Christian understanding of the cross as necessary and purposeful.
The fifth mark requires citing Daniel 7:13 (or Isaiah 53) as a named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Mark's Gospel presents Jesus mainly as a suffering servant rather than a triumphant Messiah.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; conclusion weighs the evidence and reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present.
Developing (4-6): One side more developed; few or no named sources; conclusion is descriptive.
Emerging (1-3): One-sided or very brief; minimal development.

Arguments in support: Isaiah 53 describes a 'suffering servant' — wounded for others' transgressions — which Christians apply to Jesus. The Son of Man title is used both for glory (Daniel 7:13) and for suffering/death. Mark's Gospel consistently shows the disciples failing to understand a Messiah who must suffer. The passion narrative is central to Mark's structure.
Arguments against: The baptism (Mark 1:9-11) presents a triumphant divine commissioning — the Father speaks, the Spirit descends. The Daniel 7:13 'Son of Man' is a figure of cosmic power and eternal kingship. The transfiguration (Mark 9:1-10) shows Jesus's divine glory. Mark ends with an empty tomb — resurrection implies triumph.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which John the Baptist prepared the way for Jesus in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• John preached in the desert, calling people to repent and be baptised for the forgiveness of sins.
• He pointed forward to a greater figure coming after him — someone so superior that John was not worthy to untie his sandals.
• He baptised Jesus in the River Jordan, at which point the Spirit descended and God identified Jesus as his Son.

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of the Almighty in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three characteristics with a brief explanation. Acceptable: One (absolute monotheism — the Almighty is the singular source of all existence, as stated in the Shema); Creator (brought all existence into being from nothing, forming humanity intimately as in Genesis 2); Law-Giver (source of all moral and religious law, including the Torah); Judge (holds all humanity accountable for their actions, motivating ethical living).

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Jews believe about the Shekhinah.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three points. Acceptable: Shekhinah means the divine presence, the Almighty dwelling among the Jewish people; 2 Chronicles 7:1-3 describes it filling Solomon's Temple at the dedication; it shows that the transcendent Almighty can be met in human experience; Orthodox Jews tie it closely to the Temple; Reform Jews find it wherever Jews pray and act ethically.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per belief. Belief 1: the Messiah will be a human king from the line of King David who will restore Jewish sovereignty and rebuild the Temple — he is not divine but a specially anointed human leader; this belief reflects continued trust in the Almighty's promises. Belief 2: divergent understandings of the Messiah — Orthodox Jews expect a specific future individual who will physically rebuild the Temple; Reform Jews reinterpret this as the 'messianic age' of universal justice brought by human moral effort.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which belief in the Almighty as Creator shapes Jewish life today.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: belief in the Almighty as Creator motivates environmental responsibility — creation is a gift from the Creator and Jews have a duty to protect it; this connects to Shabbat observance (rest for creation, not just humans). Way 2: belief that humanity is formed by the Almighty in an intimate act (Genesis 2 — the Almighty breathed life into Adam) gives every human being inherent dignity and worth, motivating justice and care for others. 5th mark: ‘Genesis 2 describes the Almighty forming man from dust and breathing life into him, showing the intimate relationship between Creator and creation.’

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the Messiah is the most important belief in Judaism.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Messianic hope gives Jews a future-oriented purpose and ethical motivation (tikkun olam); Jeremiah 23:5-8 anchors this in authoritative scripture; the hope for justice and universal peace is central to Jewish prayer (the Amidah includes prayers for the Messiah's coming); without this hope Judaism would lack its eschatological horizon. Arguments against: the Shema's declaration of monotheism (Deuteronomy 6:4 — 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one') is the most foundational affirmation in Judaism — recited twice daily, at deathbeds; keeping the Mitzvot (commandments) is the most practical and immediate expression of Jewish faith; the covenant relationship with the Almighty (Genesis 17, Exodus 20) is prior to any messianic belief. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Jeremiah 23:5-8 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Orthodox and Reform Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference. Difference 1: Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a specific future individual from David's line who will physically rebuild the Temple; Reform Jews tend to understand the messianic hope as a collective future era (the messianic age) rather than one specific person. Difference 2: Orthodox Jews see the coming of the Messiah as a miraculous divine act; many Reform Jews emphasise human moral effort (tikkun olam) as bringing about the conditions of justice and peace associated with the messianic age.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events from the life of the Buddha that are important to Buddhists today.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate, identified events. Acceptable points include: birth into a noble family foretold to lead to spiritual greatness; the Four Sights (encountering old age, sickness, death and a wandering ascetic); leaving the palace (the Great Renunciation); practising extreme asceticism then choosing the Middle Way; attaining enlightenment under the Bodhi tree; giving the first teaching at the Deer Park; founding the Sangha.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Buddhists believe about paticca-samuppada (dependent origination).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate points. Acceptable: all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions; nothing exists independently or permanently; when conditions change, phenomena change or cease; ignorance leads through a chain of conditions to suffering; changing the conditions can end suffering.

practice_questions.text: Explain two of the Three Marks of Existence and why they are important for Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per mark (1 for identification + development, 2 for full development). Example responses: Anicca (impermanence) — all conditioned things constantly change and eventually pass away; clinging to them as permanent causes suffering, so recognising anicca helps Buddhists reduce attachment. Anatta (no fixed self) — there is no permanent, unchanging self or soul; the ‘self’ is a label for a changing collection of processes; understanding anatta undermines ego-driven craving that causes suffering.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Milinda Panha helps Buddhists understand the teaching of anatta.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks for two developed explanations, +1 for a named source. The Milinda Panha is the named source for the 5th mark. Point 1: the chariot analogy shows that a person, like a chariot, is a label for a collection of parts — take away each part and no permanent ‘self’ remains. Point 2: the dialogue between Nagasena and King Milinda illustrates that persons exist conventionally but not ultimately — this helps Buddhists understand anatta without nihilism. 5th mark: ‘In the Milinda Panha, Nagasena uses the chariot analogy to explain to King Milinda that no fixed self exists’.

practice_questions.text:
'The Three Marks of Existence are the most important Buddhist teachings.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; weighs perspectives explicitly; conclusion justifies a clear position. Arguments in support: the Three Marks are the foundation of the Buddha's diagnosis of the human condition — understanding dukkha, anicca and anatta is the starting point for all Buddhist practice; the Milinda Panha anchors the teaching of anatta with a named authoritative source; dependent origination and the Three Marks together explain why life involves suffering and what can be done. Arguments against: the Four Noble Truths are sometimes seen as more practically central as they diagnose suffering AND prescribe the solution (the Eightfold Path); the Three Refuges (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) give structure to daily Buddhist life and may matter more practically; Mahayana Buddhists might prioritise the Bodhisattva ideal or sunyata over the Three Marks. Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least the Milinda Panha named. Developing (4-6): One side only or very brief treatment of the other. Emerging (1-3): One-sided or very brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the Buddha's enlightenment is significant for Buddhists today.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate points. Acceptable: the enlightenment proved it is possible for a human being to achieve liberation from suffering; it established the Dhamma as an authoritative body of teaching; it led to the founding of the Sangha community; it provides a model for Buddhist practice — following the Buddha’s Middle Way; it is commemorated at the festival of Wesak; it shows that nibbana can be reached in this lifetime.

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of Brahman in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate characteristics. Acceptable: ultimate reality/absolute truth underlying all existence; present everywhere (Nirguna — formless and attributeless); present within every being as Antaryami; known as a personal God through Bhagavan; source of all creation; described in the Upanishads (Katha Upanishad 2.2.6-8) as the eternal reality in which all the worlds rest; eternal, unchanging.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between Nirguna Brahman and Saguna Brahman.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Nirguna Brahman: formless, without qualities or attributes, beyond description — Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1-2 (1 mark). Saguna Brahman: Brahman with qualities, personal, able to be worshipped — Rig Veda 1.154 describes Vishnu as a Saguna form (1 mark). Relationship: these are not two gods but two ways of understanding the same ultimate reality (1 mark). Practice: most Hindus approach Saguna Brahman through murti and the deities, while Nirguna Brahman is approached through meditation and study (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two of the three aspects of the divine in Hinduism (Brahman, Antaryami and Bhagavan).
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per aspect. Antaryami: God dwelling within the heart of every being as the inner witness and controller — this teaches Hindus that the divine is not distant but intimately present within every person, motivating inner reverence and prayer. Bhagavan: Brahman as the personal loving God beyond the world, the God of devotion (bhakti) — this enables Hindus to have a personal loving relationship with the divine through worship and devotion.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Hindus understand and worship Vishnu.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: Vishnu is the preserver of cosmic order (dharma) who manifests through avatars (such as Rama and Krishna) when dharma is threatened — this gives devotees a focus for personal devotion and moral example. Way 2: Vishnu is worshipped in temples through murti (sacred image) where he is understood as Bhagavan — the personal God who can receive devotion. 5th mark: Rig Veda 1.22 describes Vishnu’s three cosmic strides that measure the universe; or Rig Veda 1.154 describes Vishnu as Saguna Brahman.

practice_questions.text:
'Nirguna Brahman is more important than Saguna Brahman in Hinduism.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Nirguna Brahman represents the deepest philosophical understanding of the divine as beyond all human attributes; the Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1-2 points to Brahman beyond speech and thought; the Advaita Vedanta school (Shankara) argues that Nirguna is the ultimate truth and Saguna is a lower-level approximation for devotees who cannot yet grasp formless reality. Arguments against: Saguna Brahman enables the loving devotional relationship (bhakti) that is central to most Hindus' practice; the Rig Veda 1.154 presents Vishnu in personal form accessible to worshippers; Vaishnavism argues that Bhagavan (personal God) is the highest truth, not an inferior form; for most practising Hindus, worship of deities in their Saguna forms (murti in temples, home shrines, festivals) is how Brahman is experienced. Secure (7-9): Both sides with some development; at least one scripture named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three roles of Shakti (the divine feminine) in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: consort of Shiva as Parvati, representing love and devotion; consort of Vishnu as Lakshmi, representing prosperity and grace; the dynamic power or energy through which Brahman creates and maintains the universe; worshipped in Shaktism as the supreme divine; manifestations include Durga (warrior goddess) and Kali.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that Surah al-Fatiha (Surah 1) teaches Muslims about Allah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Allah is the Lord of all worlds — he has authority over and created all that exists.
• Allah is both Ar-Rahman (universally merciful) and Ar-Rahim (specifically merciful to believers) — mercy is his defining characteristic.
• Allah is the Master of the Day of Judgement — all will ultimately be accountable to him.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that Muslims believe about Tawhid.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Tawhid means the absolute oneness and uniqueness of Allah — there is no god but Allah.
• It rules out all partners, equals, offspring or rivals to Allah — ascribing partners is the greatest sin (shirk).
• It is expressed in the Shahadah: 'There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his messenger', which every Muslim recites.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the 99 names of Allah help Muslims understand who Allah is.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• The name Al-Khaliq (the Creator) tells Muslims that Allah is the sole originator of all things — nothing in creation made itself, and this gives human life meaning and purpose as part of Allah's deliberate creation.
• The name Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) tells Muslims that Allah continually covers and forgives sin for those who repent — this shapes Muslim prayer practice, encouraging honest confession and trust in divine forgiveness.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two differences between the names Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Ar-Rahman refers to Allah's universal, overflowing mercy — it is extended to all creation, believer and non-believer alike, sustaining the world in existence. It is found in Surah 55:1, the one word that opens the surah: 'Ar-Rahman'.
• Ar-Rahim refers to the specific mercy Allah shows particularly to believers — the mercy of forgiveness, spiritual reward, and paradise for those who submit to his will. It is found in Surah 3:31.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 55:1 (for Ar-Rahman) or Surah 3:31 (for Ar-Rahim) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Tawhid is the foundational belief — without it, no other Islamic practice makes sense. The Shahadah (declaration of faith) begins with Tawhid. Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is described in the Qur'an as the one sin that cannot be forgiven if died upon. Every Five Pillar is an expression of Tawhid — directing worship and obedience to Allah alone.
Against: Some Muslims might argue prophethood (Risalah) is equally foundational — without the Prophet Muhammad, the Qur'an would not have been revealed and Tawhid itself would not be known. Others might argue the Day of Judgement (Akhirah) is the most practically motivating belief, since it shapes daily ethical choices. Non-religious thinkers would question whether any religious belief is 'important' in an objective sense, arguing that ethics and compassion are what truly matter.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the 99 names of Allah are important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Muslims use the names in dhikr (remembrance) — reciting them with prayer beads deepens their knowledge of and love for Allah.
• The names shape Islamic ethics: because Allah is Ar-Razzaq (the Sustainer), Muslims are encouraged to be generous with wealth, knowing it ultimately comes from Allah.
• Specific names are called upon in different types of prayer: Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) in prayers for forgiveness, As-Salam (the Source of Peace) in prayers for comfort.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Christians believe about the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) God is one being in three co-equal Persons; (2) The three Persons are Father, Son and Holy Spirit; (3) The Trinity is expressed in the Nicene Creed agreed at Nicaea (325 CE). Each must be a separately identifiable point.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about the Incarnation.
practice_questions.marks: May include: the eternal Son of God became human in Jesus; John 1:14 — 'the Word became flesh'; 1 Timothy 3:16 calls it 'the mystery of our religion'; Jesus is both fully God and fully human; the Incarnation is the basis for the Christmas celebration. Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways Christians interpret the account of creation in Genesis.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Literal interpretation — some Christians, especially evangelical or fundamentalist Protestants, understand the six days as historical days; God created the universe in six 24-hour periods; this is sometimes called Young Earth Creationism; (2) Metaphorical interpretation — many mainline Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox Christians read Genesis as theological poetry that conveys truths about God's nature and humanity's relationship with God, rather than a scientific account; this allows compatibility with evolutionary biology. Development beyond naming the view required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about salvation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Salvation comes through Christ alone — Acts 4:8–12 records Peter stating 'there is salvation in no one else' but Jesus; (2) God's motive for salvation is love — John 3:16 teaches that God gave his only Son so that all who believe would not perish but have eternal life. The 5th mark requires a named source: Acts 4:8–12, or John 3:16.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events in Jesus' last days as recorded in Luke 22–24.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete events: (1) The Last Supper — Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples; (2) Arrest and crucifixion — betrayed by Judas, tried by Pilate, crucified at Golgotha; (3) The resurrection — the empty tomb is found by the women; the risen Jesus appears to disciples.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important Christian belief is the resurrection of Jesus.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicitly weighs; justified conclusion. FOR: without the resurrection, the cross is merely a tragic death; 1 Corinthians 15 argues 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile'; resurrection is the basis of Christian hope. AGAINST: the Incarnation may be considered more foundational (without it the cross has no saving significance); others argue the Trinity is the organising belief; some emphasise the teaching of Jesus (e.g. the Sermon on the Mount) as equally central to Christian identity. Named sources: Luke 24; 1 Corinthians 15; John 3:16; Acts 4:8–12. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- The Trinity consists of three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
- The three persons are co-equal and co-eternal, sharing one divine nature.
- The Trinity is expressed in the Nicene Creed (325/381 AD).
- Matthew 3:13-17 (the baptism of Jesus) shows all three persons of the Trinity present simultaneously.
- The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father (and, in Western traditions, the Son — the Filioque clause).
Do not award marks for points that conflate two ideas into one or simply restate one idea in different words.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways Christians use the Nicene Creed to express belief in the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content for up to 3 marks:
- The Nicene Creed was formulated at the Council of Nicaea (325 AD) and expanded at Constantinople (381 AD).
- It affirms one God and describes Jesus as 'true God from true God, begotten not made'.
- It is recited in Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant services as a shared statement of faith.
- It describes the Holy Spirit as 'the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father'.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the incarnation is important for Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required — a bare statement earns 1 mark per point; development earns 2 marks per point.

Acceptable explanations:
- The incarnation reveals what God is like in human terms: because Jesus was fully human, Christians believe they can understand God's nature (loving, compassionate, suffering with people) through reading the Gospels. This means the incarnation makes God accessible rather than remote.
- The incarnation gives Christians confidence that Jesus understands human suffering: because he experienced hunger, grief and pain, he can intercede for believers with genuine empathy (as described in Hebrews 4:15, though students are not required to cite this). This encourages Christians to pray and trust God in difficult times.
- The incarnation is the basis of salvation: God becoming human was necessary for Jesus to die as a human sacrifice and rise again, breaking the power of sin. Without the incarnation, atonement could not happen.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about creation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Christians believe God created the universe and declared it 'very good' — creation is not evil or accidental but the deliberate act of a loving, all-powerful God. Genesis 1-3 is the primary scriptural source for this belief.
- Christians interpret the creation account in divergent ways: some read Genesis 1 literally (six 24-hour days), while others read it metaphorically (theological truth, not scientific description). John 1:1-18 presents a complementary account showing that the divine Word (Jesus) was active in creation from the beginning: 'Through him all things were made.'

The 5th mark requires a named source: 'According to Genesis 1...' or 'John 1:1-18 states...' or 'Dei Verbum (Vatican II document on Scripture) teaches that...' Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The Trinity is the most important Christian belief.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; weighs perspectives explicitly; conclusion justifies a clear position. Example: argues that the Trinity is foundational because all other doctrines (incarnation, atonement, the Church) depend on a Trinitarian God, supported by the Nicene Creed; then argues that salvation/atonement could be considered more important because it is the most personally relevant belief for Christians today, supported by John 3:16 or Acts 4:12; conclusion explains which side is stronger and why.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present but may be thin.

Developing (4-6): One side developed more than the other; sources vague or absent; conclusion descriptive not evaluative.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided or very brief; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- The Trinity is the defining feature of Christianity that distinguishes it from other monotheistic faiths: Islam and Judaism affirm one God but reject the Trinity; the Nicene Creed makes Trinitarian belief the test of orthodox Christian faith.
- All other Christian doctrines depend on the Trinity: the incarnation requires a Son who can take flesh; salvation requires the Father who sends, the Son who dies, and the Spirit who applies grace; without the Trinity, these doctrines collapse.
- The baptism of Jesus (Matthew 3:13-17) shows the Trinity revealed by God himself — not a human invention but a divine self-disclosure.

Arguments against:
- The resurrection could be considered more important: Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15 that 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile.' The resurrection is the event that validates everything Christians believe; without it, the Trinity is simply an abstract doctrine with no saving power.
- For many Christians in practice, the most important belief is salvation — that God forgives sins through Christ. This is the belief that transforms daily life. The Trinity, while true, is an intellectual framework; salvation is personally experienced.
- Some Protestant Christians (Baptists, for example) de-emphasise creedal statements in favour of personal faith, suggesting that the Trinity as a formal doctrine is less central to everyday Christian identity than trust in Jesus.

SPaG note: technical terms like 'Trinity', 'incarnation', 'Nicene Creed' and 'monotheistic' must be spelt correctly to earn SPaG marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the baptism of Jesus (Matthew 3:13-17) is important for Christian belief in the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- It is the clearest biblical moment where all three persons of the Trinity are simultaneously present: Jesus (the Son) is baptised, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father's voice declares 'This is my Son, whom I love.' This gives Christians scriptural evidence that the Trinity is not a later invention but grounded in Jesus's own life.
- It shows the distinct roles of the three persons: the Son is obedient and submissive to baptism; the Spirit empowers and descends; the Father affirms and declares. This teaches Christians that the three persons relate to each other and are genuinely distinct, not just three names for the same undifferentiated God.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about revelation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: God has revealed himself through the prophets and scriptures (1); the covenants with Noah and Abraham are key moments of revelation showing God's faithfulness and personal concern (1); Jesus Christ is the fullest and final revelation of God — Hebrews 1:1-4 (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Christians believe happened at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Jesus took Peter, James and John up a mountain (1); his face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light; Moses and Elijah appeared with him (1); God's voice declared from a cloud 'This is my Son whom I love — listen to him' (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe the covenants with Noah and Abraham provide evidence for God's existence.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: The covenant with Noah shows God's care and faithfulness to all creation — God promises never to destroy all life by flood again, revealing a personal God who acts in history (2); the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15) is a visionary encounter in which God promises descendants as numerous as the stars, showing God initiates personal relationships and makes binding promises (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe miracles provide evidence for the existence of God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The healing in John 4:43-54 — where the official's son recovered at the exact moment Jesus spoke — suggests God has power over natural processes, supporting belief in an omnipotent creator (2); miracles produce faith in those who witness them, suggesting they originate from a divine source rather than natural coincidence (2); source credit for citing John 4:43-54 or Hebrews 1:1-4 explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Miracles and visions prove that God exists.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: miracles (John 4:43-54) and visions (Genesis 15, Matthew 17:1-13) show God communicating directly; transformed lives and unexplained healings support this. Counter: Hume's argument that natural law always makes doubt more rational than acceptance; Dawkins on visions as brain chemistry; only anecdote supports miracles. Evaluate which position is stronger with reasoning. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: revelation, covenant, Transfiguration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two divergent Christian views about visions, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Catholic Christianity formally evaluates reported visions through the Church's Magisterium — only approved visions are accepted as reliable, with Hebrews 1:1-4 confirming that any vision must align with Christ as the fullness of revelation (2); many Protestant Christians hold that scripture (sola scriptura) is the sole reliable source of revelation, so personal visions should always be tested against biblical teaching — the Transfiguration (Matthew 17) is paradigmatic but personal visions today are secondary to scripture (2); source credit for Hebrews 1:1-4 or Matthew 17:1-13 explicitly named (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about the Qur'an as revelation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: the Qur'an is the direct speech of Allah, transmitted through the angel Jibril to Muhammad (1); it is the final and complete revelation, superseding earlier scriptures (1); its Arabic text is the literal word of Allah — translations are interpretations, not the Qur'an itself (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Muslims believe about the vision in Surah 19:16-22.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the angel Jibril appeared to Maryam (the Virgin Mary) in human form (1); he announced the miraculous birth of Isa (Jesus) — a child to be born without a human father, by divine command (1); this vision is significant because it confirms both the reality of divine communication through visions and the elevated status of Maryam and Isa in Islamic theology (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims believe the Qur'an is a miracle.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Surah 17:88 issues the challenge that no human or group could produce a text equal to the Qur'an — and in 1,400 years no convincing human response to this challenge has been produced (2); the Qur'an's internal consistency, its Arabic literary perfection, and its preservation without corruption over fourteen centuries are presented as evidence that no human author could have produced it (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim reasons for believing the Qur'an provides evidence for the existence of Allah, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Surah 17:84-89 challenges all humanity to produce a text equal to the Qur'an — Muslims argue that the inimitability of the Qur'an is a standing miracle proving its divine origin (2); the Qur'an's ability to transform individuals and communities — from 7th-century Arabia to contemporary Muslims worldwide — suggests a source beyond human authorship (2); source credit for Surah 17:84-89 or Surah 34:46-50 named explicitly with surah number (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The Qur'an as a miracle is the most convincing argument that Allah exists.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Muslim case: Surah 17:88 — the inimitability challenge; 1,400-year preservation; transformation of individuals and communities. Counter: atheists argue beauty in a text is not proof of divine authorship; other traditions also claim their scriptures are uniquely authoritative; psychological explanations for visions exist. Evaluate whether the Qur'an as miracle is stronger or weaker than other arguments (design, cosmological, religious experience). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, surah named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: revelation, inimitability, Qur'an, Maryam.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Sunni, Shi'a and Sufi Muslims may differ in their understanding of revelation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Sunni Muslims emphasise the authority of the Qur'an and Sunnah as the complete and final revelation — Surah 34:46-50 establishes this — and the role of scholarly consensus (ijma) in interpreting it (2); Sufi Muslims seek not merely intellectual understanding of Qur'anic revelation but transformative personal encounter with Allah — dhikr (remembrance) practices aim to make the reality of Allah's presence known in direct experience (2); source credit for Surah 34:46-50 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about what happens after death.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) The soul undergoes particular judgement immediately after death; (2) Those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified enter purgatory; (3) At the Last Day the body and soul are reunited for the general judgement. Each must be a separate identifiable point.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the Paschal Mystery.
practice_questions.marks: Responses may include: suffering/death/resurrection/ascension of Jesus; derived from Passover (Pesach); bodily resurrection confirmed by the empty tomb (Luke 24); redemptive significance — liberation from sin; celebrated centrally in the Mass. Three accurate relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic teachings about purgatory and how it differs from Protestant beliefs.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations required. E.g. (1) Purgatory is a state of purification after death for souls who die in God's grace — it means Catholics pray for the dead and offer Masses for them; (2) Most Protestant churches reject purgatory, arguing it is not supported by Scripture — the 39 Articles call it 'a fond thing vainly invented'. Development beyond a bare statement required for both points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic beliefs about salvation and grace, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Salvation is through Christ alone — Acts 4:8–12 records Peter stating 'there is salvation in no one else'; (2) Grace is God's unearned gift received through faith and the sacraments. The 5th mark requires a named source: Acts 4:8–12, or John 3:16.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways Luke 24 shows that the resurrection was a real, bodily event.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points: (1) The tomb was found empty; (2) The risen Jesus walked and talked with disciples on the road to Emmaus; (3) Jesus revealed himself in the breaking of bread (he ate with disciples).

practice_questions.text: 'Belief in purgatory is the most distinctive Catholic teaching about life after death.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; weighs perspectives explicitly; justified conclusion. FOR: purgatory is distinctively Catholic — Orthodox and most Protestant Churches reject it; it shapes Catholic practice (prayers for the dead, Masses for the departed, All Souls Day); rooted in 2 Corinthians 5:1–10 and Church Tradition. AGAINST: others might argue resurrection itself (John 11:17–27) or heaven and hell are more fundamental; some would say the Paschal Mystery as a whole, not just purgatory, is the most distinctive belief. Secure (7–9): both sides, some development, at least one source. Developing (4–6): one-sided. Emerging (1–3): minimal.

practice_questions.text: Outline three roles of angels (Malaikah) in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete roles, e.g. (1) Jibril — the angel of revelation, who brought the Qur'an to Muhammad; (2) Izra'il — the angel of death, who takes the soul at death (Surah 32:11); (3) Kiraman Katibin — the two recording angels who note every human deed, which will be presented at judgement. Three separately identifiable roles.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about al-Qadr (predestination).
practice_questions.marks: May include: al-Qadr is one of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam; Allah has complete foreknowledge of all events; the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 teaches that each person's fate is 'written' by an angel before birth; humans still have moral responsibility and are judged for their choices; Shi'a Islam stresses Adl (divine justice) and human free will. Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about life after death (Akhirah).
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Bodily resurrection — on the Last Day Allah will raise all the dead, regardless of what has happened to the body; Surah 17 responds to sceptics asking how God can raise decomposed bones; (2) Judgement — each person's deeds are weighed on scales (mizan) and the recording angels' books are opened; Allah's mercy also plays a decisive role. Development beyond bare statements required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about Malaikah, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Jibril is the angel of revelation — Surah 2:97–98 states he brought the Qur'an down upon the heart of Muhammad; without Jibril Muslims would have no Qur'an; (2) Izra'il is the angel of death — Surah 32:11 describes him as 'entrusted with you', taking the soul at the appointed time. 5th mark requires a named source: Surah 2:97–98 or Surah 32:11.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between Muslim and Catholic Christian beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete contrasts: (1) Islam has no purgatory; Catholicism teaches purgatory as a state of purification after death; (2) In Islam, judgement is based on deeds weighed on scales (mizan) with divine mercy; in Christianity, salvation comes through faith in Christ's atoning sacrifice; (3) Islam emphasises barzakh (waiting state between death and judgement); most Christian denominations have no equivalent concept.

practice_questions.text: 'Muslim and Christian beliefs about life after death are more similar than different.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. FOR: both teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, and eternal destinations (Jannah/heaven, Jahannam/hell); both hold that earthly life shapes eternal destiny; both see God/Allah as just and merciful in judgement. AGAINST: purgatory (Catholic Christianity) is absent from Islam; Christianity grounds salvation in Christ's atonement — a concept absent from Islamic theology; the role of the Imam in Shi'a Islam has no Christian equivalent; Protestant Christianity (39 Articles) and Islamic teaching both reject purgatory but for different reasons. Named sources: Surah 17:49–72; 2 Corinthians 5:1–10; 39 Articles. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the covenant between the Almighty and Abraham (Genesis 17).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features. Acceptable: the Almighty promised Abraham a great nation of descendants; the Almighty promised the land of Canaan (the Promised Land) to Abraham's descendants; circumcision was established as the physical sign of the covenant; the Almighty established a special ongoing relationship with Abraham's descendants; the covenant was renewed with Isaac and Jacob.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the principle of Pikuach Nefesh.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three points. Acceptable: preserving life takes precedence over almost all other commandments; nefesh means life or soul; Talmud Yoma 83-84 teaches that Shabbat may be broken to save a life; a Jewish doctor may work on Shabbat to treat a patient; a pregnant woman need not fast on Yom Kippur if fasting would endanger her.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Mitzvot shape the daily life of Jewish people today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: kashrut (food laws as part of the Mitzvot) shapes what a Jew eats at every meal, requiring separate utensils for meat and dairy, avoiding non-kosher foods; this daily discipline creates a constant reminder of the covenant and Jewish identity. Way 2: Shabbat observance (commanded in the Decalogue at Exodus 20) shapes one day every week — from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday, work is forbidden; families gather, synagogue is attended, and the rhythm of holy time structures the week.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Jewish teachings about life after death.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Teaching 1: Orthodox Judaism teaches bodily resurrection (techiyat ha-meitim) — the dead will be raised in the Messianic age; this is tied to the collective redemption of the Jewish people. Teaching 2: Reform Judaism tends to emphasise the spiritual legacy of how one lived rather than physical resurrection — the focus is on living ethically now; some Reform Jews believe in the soul's return to the Almighty. 5th mark: ‘Ecclesiastes 12 reflects on human mortality and states that the spirit returns to the Almighty who gave it.’

practice_questions.text:
'Jewish beliefs about life after death are less important than Christian beliefs.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Jewish scripture (Torah) focuses primarily on this life and ethical behaviour rather than the afterlife; Jewish practice centres on covenant, commandments and tikkun olam in the present; the ambiguity of Ecclesiastes 12 suggests afterlife is not a central doctrinal concern; some Jewish thinkers argue that excessive focus on afterlife rewards distorts moral motivation. Arguments against: Orthodox Judaism has detailed and important beliefs about resurrection, Olam Ha-Ba and Gehinnom; the messianic hope (Jeremiah 23:5-8) includes collective eschatology; Christian afterlife beliefs (John 11:25 — resurrection; John 3:16 — eternal life) are explicitly tied to faith in Christ — one tradition's afterlife emphasis does not automatically make another's less important; many Orthodox Jews see resurrection as central to Jewish faith. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Ecclesiastes 12 or John 11:25 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Maimonides' Mishneh Torah is important in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason. Reason 1: the Mishneh Torah systematised all 613 Mitzvot for the first time in a single, comprehensive, accessible code — it made the vast body of Jewish law navigable for ordinary Jews; the Sefer Madda established the philosophical foundations of why Jews observe the Mitzvot. Reason 2: Maimonides (1138-1204 CE) was the foremost legal and philosophical authority of medieval Judaism — his 13 Principles of Faith, set out in his commentary on the Mishnah, became widely accepted as a summary of core Jewish belief, and the Mishneh Torah carried that authority into every area of Jewish law.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events in the last days of Jesus's life.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points from: Last Supper, betrayal, arrest, trial before Pilate, crucifixion, death, burial, resurrection, ascension. Each must be a separate identifiable event — do not award a single mark for a narrative sentence covering multiple events.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about the resurrection of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day after the crucifixion.
- The empty tomb was discovered by women followers, as described in Luke 24:1-12.
- The risen Jesus appeared to his disciples before his ascension.
- The resurrection is the foundation of Christian hope — without it Paul says 'your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17).
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the crucifixion is important for Christian beliefs about salvation.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The crucifixion is where Christians believe Jesus took the penalty for human sin: through his death, the broken relationship between God and humanity is restored. This means the cross is not a defeat but the central act of God's saving plan.
- The crucifixion demonstrates the depth of God's love: Jesus was willing to suffer and die for sinners, showing that God's grace is freely given, not earned. This motivates Christians to respond in faith and gratitude rather than trying to earn their own salvation.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about salvation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Christians believe salvation is found exclusively in Jesus Christ: Peter declares in Acts 4:8-12 that 'Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.' This means Christians believe faith in Jesus is the only route to restored relationship with God.
- Christians believe salvation is received through faith, not earned by human effort: John 3:16-21 records Jesus teaching Nicodemus that those who believe in the Son of God will not perish but have eternal life — a gift of God's grace (sola fide in Protestant tradition).

The 5th mark: the source must be named (Acts 4:8-12, John 3:16-21, or another specific reference). A vague phrase like 'the Bible teaches salvation' does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The resurrection is more important than the crucifixion for Christian faith.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing of perspectives; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support (resurrection more important):
- Paul argues that the resurrection is the proof that Jesus is who he claimed to be and that the cross worked: 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins' (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, the cross is merely a tragic death.
- The resurrection is the basis of Christian hope for life after death: because Jesus rose, Christians believe they too will rise. The ascension follows from the resurrection, giving Jesus his role as intercessor at God's right hand.
- Many Protestant theologians argue that Easter Sunday is more fundamental than Good Friday in the Christian calendar — the cross only makes sense in the light of the empty tomb.

Arguments against (crucifixion equally or more important):
- The cross is where the actual work of salvation takes place: Jesus bears the consequence of sin and makes reconciliation possible. Acts 4:8-12 and John 3:16-21 point to belief in the crucified Christ as the means of salvation — not the resurrection as a separate event.
- Many atonement theologies (penal substitution, Christus Victor, moral influence) are primarily focused on what happens at the cross, not the resurrection. The resurrection validates but does not replace the cross.
- Some Christians argue the two events are inseparable: the 'Paschal Mystery' (a Catholic term used across denominations) refers to both together as one saving event. Separating them misunderstands the doctrine.

SPaG note: 'resurrection', 'crucifixion', 'ascension', 'atonement' must be spelt correctly for SPaG marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Protestant and Catholic beliefs about how salvation works.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Protestants emphasise sola fide (faith alone): salvation is received through faith in Christ, not through performing sacraments or good works. Catholics teach that grace is communicated through the seven sacraments (CCC 1210-1211) and that works done in grace are genuinely meritorious.
- Protestants generally recognise two sacraments (baptism and the Lord's Supper/Eucharist), commanded by Jesus in the Gospels. Catholics recognise seven sacraments as channels of grace. This reflects a different understanding of how God's saving grace reaches individuals.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of the believer as described in Surah al-Baqarah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Believers believe in the unseen — they trust in Allah, angels, and the hereafter without direct sensory proof.
• They establish regular prayer (salah) — their faith is expressed through structured, daily acts of worship.
• They give from what Allah has provided — their belief is shown in generosity and care for others.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen in the story of Adam as khalifah in Surah 2:30-39.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Allah announced to the angels that he would create a vicegerent (khalifah) on earth; the angels questioned this because humans would cause corruption.
• Adam was taught the names of all things and the angels were commanded to bow to him — all did except Iblis, who refused.
• Adam and his wife were placed in a garden, tempted by Iblis, and sent to earth when they disobeyed; Allah forgave Adam when he repented.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Qur'anic creation account shows what Allah is like.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Creation demonstrates Allah's absolute power — the concept of Kun fa-yakun ('Be! And it is') in passages like Surah 41:11 shows that Allah creates simply by speaking; nothing can resist or limit his creative command.
• Creation is a sign pointing to Allah — Surah 45:3-5 describes the alternation of night and day, the provision of rain and the diversity of creation as signs for 'people of understanding'; Allah communicates his existence through the natural world.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the concept of khalifah affects how Muslims live today.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Khalifah means Muslims see themselves as stewards of the earth, not its owners — they are accountable to Allah for how they treat the environment, giving Islamic support for conservation and opposition to wasteful consumption.
• Khalifah also extends to social justice: as stewards, Muslims are responsible for the fair distribution of wealth and care for the vulnerable — this connects to the payment of zakah and the commitment to justice found throughout Surah 2.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 2:30 (or the khalifah passage) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The Qur'anic teaching that humans are khalifah is the most important teaching about human beings in Islam.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Khalifah establishes humanity's unique relationship with Allah — above the angels (who bowed to Adam), trusted with the earth, accountable at Judgement. It underpins both environmental ethics and social justice in Islam. The passage (Surah 2:30-39) is foundational for understanding human dignity and responsibility.
Against: Some would argue the doctrine of Tawhid is more fundamental — without understanding who Allah is, the concept of human stewardship has no context. Others might argue the Five Pillars are the most important expression of what it means to be human in Islam — they define the practical shape of Muslim life. Non-religious thinkers would question any teaching that grants humans a unique divine-given role, arguing that humans are simply one species among many with no special mandate.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Surah al-Baqarah describes non-believers and hypocrites.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Non-believers are described as having 'sealed hearts' — they will not respond to warning because they have hardened themselves against truth.
• Their hearing and sight are described as covered — they cannot receive the message of the Qur'an.
• Hypocrites claim to believe but do not — the Qur'an treats them as more dangerous than open unbelievers because they corrupt the community from within.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Christians believe in the resurrection of the body after death.
- Christians believe in a final judgement where each person faces accountability for their earthly life.
- Christians believe in heaven — eternal life in God's presence.
- Christians believe in hell — eternal separation from God.
- Catholic (and some Orthodox) Christians believe in purgatory — purification for souls not yet fully holy.
- Protestant traditions (39 Articles) reject purgatory.
Each point must be identifiably distinct — not three sentences rephrasing the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the 39 Articles of Religion teach about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- The 39 Articles affirm belief in the resurrection of the body.
- They affirm eternal life in heaven for the saved.
- Article XXII explicitly rejects purgatory as 'a fond thing vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.'
- They reflect the Protestant (Anglican) position that heaven and hell are the only post-mortem destinations.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the problem of evil challenges Christian belief in God.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Moral evil (caused by human choices — war, murder, cruelty) challenges belief in an omnipotent God: if God is all-powerful, why does he allow humans to choose to harm each other? Some conclude that either God is not all-powerful, or he does not care.
- Natural evil (earthquakes, disease, floods) challenges belief in a benevolent God: unlike moral evil, natural evil cannot be blamed on human free will. A truly loving God could apparently design a world without natural disasters. Its existence seems incompatible with a creator who is both powerful and good.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian responses to the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- The free will defence (Augustine): God gave humans genuine freedom; moral evil is the result of that freedom being misused. God is not responsible for choices made by free creatures. A world with free will is better than a world of moral robots, even if free will is misused.
- The soul-making theodicy (Irenaeus, developed by John Hick in Evil and the God of Love, 1966): suffering is the necessary condition for moral and spiritual growth. The world is a 'vale of soul-making' — if everything were comfortable, humans would never develop courage, compassion or faith. Psalm 119 reflects this: 'It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees.'

The 5th mark: name a source — 'John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966)', 'Psalm 103', 'Psalm 119', '2 Corinthians 5:1-10', or the book of Job. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The vale of soul-making is the most convincing Christian response to the problem of evil.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources (Hick, Augustine, scripture); explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- The soul-making theodicy explains both moral and natural evil: both are necessary conditions for humans to develop virtues like courage, compassion and faith. It is more comprehensive than the free will defence, which only addresses moral evil.
- John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) grounds soul-making in Irenaeus's theology (c.130-202 CE) — the idea that humans are created immature and grow towards 'the likeness of God.' This gives the theodicy deep roots in Christian tradition, not just modern philosophy.
- The Bible supports the idea that suffering has a developmental purpose: Psalm 119 states 'It was good for me to be afflicted'; the book of Job ends not with an explanation of Job's suffering but with his deepened encounter with God.

Arguments against:
- The soul-making theodicy struggles with extreme suffering (Holocaust, childhood cancer) that goes far beyond any plausible 'educational' purpose. John Hick himself acknowledged this weakness. A child who dies in agony before developing moral character cannot easily be said to have 'benefited' from suffering.
- Augustine's free will defence has strong scriptural grounding in the Fall narrative (Genesis 3) and Paul's teaching on original sin. For many Christians this is more convincing because it identifies a cause of evil (human rebellion) rather than asking victims to find meaning in their pain.
- Non-religious critics argue that both theodicies are post-hoc rationalisations — invented to protect belief in God rather than genuine explanations. The problem of evil, they argue, gives good reason to conclude there is no God.
