- Both theodicies leave natural evil partially unexplained. If God could have made a world without earthquakes or disease but chose not to, soul-making does not fully answer why.

SPaG: 'theodicy', 'eschatology', 'omnipotent', 'benevolent' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities between Christian and Islamic beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that after death all people will face judgement by God: Christians believe they will appear before 'the judgment seat of Christ' (2 Corinthians 5:10); Muslims believe their deeds will be weighed on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din).
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that the outcome of judgement is either heaven or hell: Christians describe heaven as eternal life in God's presence; Islamic teaching describes Paradise (Jannah) as a state of joy and divine favour. Both traditions describe hell as a place of punishment for the unrepentant.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the Four Noble Truths.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate, identified truths with a brief explanation. Dukkha: suffering/unsatisfactoriness exists; Samudaya: suffering has a cause (tanha/craving); Nirodha: suffering can cease (nibbana); Magga: there is a path to the cessation of suffering (the Eightfold Path / Middle Way).

practice_questions.text: Outline three parts of the Threefold Way in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate points. Acceptable: sila (ethical conduct) covers Right Speech, Right Action and Right Livelihood; samadhi (mental development) covers Right Effort, Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration; panna (wisdom) covers Right Understanding and Right Intention.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Buddhist teachings about why suffering arises.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching (1 for identification, 2 for development). Teaching 1: tanha (craving) — the Second Noble Truth identifies craving for sensory pleasure, existence and non-existence as the root of suffering; clinging to things as permanent causes inevitable disappointment. Teaching 2: the Three Poisons (greed, hatred, delusion) — these are depicted at the centre of the Wheel of Life as driving beings through samsara; they fuel tanha and keep beings trapped in conditioned existence.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Buddhist beliefs about nibbana.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks for two developed explanations, +1 for naming the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Belief 1: nibbana is the cessation of tanha (craving) — when all craving is extinguished, the causes of suffering and rebirth in samsara end. Belief 2: nibbana differs between Theravada and Mahayana — Theravada sees it as individual liberation, while Mahayana Bodhisattvas delay personal nibbana to help all sentient beings. 5th mark: ‘The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta records the Buddha teaching nirodha — the cessation of tanha — as the Third Noble Truth.’

practice_questions.text:
'The Eightfold Path is the most important part of the Four Noble Truths.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; conclusion justifies a position. Arguments in support: the Eightfold Path is the practical prescription without which the other truths are just theory; it covers all aspects of life (ethics, meditation, wisdom) through the Threefold Way; it is the Middle Way that the Buddha himself followed to enlightenment. Arguments against: without understanding dukkha (First Truth) there is no motivation to practise; identifying tanha as the cause (Second Truth) diagnoses the specific problem the path addresses; nibbana as the goal (Third Truth) gives the path its meaning — without the destination the path is directionless; some argue that the Second Truth’s diagnosis of tanha is the most fundamental insight. Secure (7-9): Both sides with some development; Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Very brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three aspects of the Eightfold Path.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three correctly identified aspects. Any three from: Right Understanding, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration. Brief explanation earns the mark; full development is not required.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Hindu teachings about the atman.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate points. Acceptable: the atman is the eternal individual self or soul within every being; it is divine in nature, related to or identical with Brahman; it transmigrates through samsara at death, taking a new body shaped by karma; the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4 describes the atman's journey after death; it is not the ego or personality but the deepest unchanging core; liberation (moksha) occurs when the atman is freed from karma.

practice_questions.text: Describe the four aims of life (Purusharthas) in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Naming all four earns up to 2 marks: dharma (duty/righteousness), artha (wealth/prosperity), kama (pleasure/desire), moksha (liberation). Development earns up to 2 marks: dharma is the most foundational, governing how artha and kama should be pursued; moksha is the ultimate spiritual goal; Bhagavad Gita 3.35 emphasises following one's own dharma.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Hindu teachings about how karma affects the cycle of samsara.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching. Teaching 1: good karma (from ethical actions) leads to better future lives — the atman is reborn in higher forms, closer to liberation; bad karma leads to lower rebirths. Teaching 2: karma drives the cycle of samsara itself — as long as desires and ignorance generate new karma, the atman continues to be reborn; only when karma is exhausted through dharmic living and devotion can moksha be achieved.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Hindu beliefs about moksha (liberation from samsara).
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Belief 1: moksha is liberation from the cycle of samsara — the atman is freed from the bondage of karma and desire, ending the cycle of death and rebirth. Belief 2: there are different understandings of moksha — Advaita Vedanta sees it as the atman realising its identity with Brahman; Vaishnavism sees it as the atman entering Vaikuntha and dwelling eternally with Vishnu/Bhagavan. 5th mark: ‘The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4 describes how karma shapes the atman’s journey through rebirth toward liberation.’

practice_questions.text:
'The Hindu belief in samsara gives life more meaning than the Christian belief in resurrection.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: samsara gives every action moral weight across many lifetimes — karma means justice is always served; the Purusharthas give a structured framework for the whole of life including multiple lives; moksha as the ultimate goal provides long-term spiritual purpose. Arguments against: Christianity’s belief in one life and resurrection (John 11:25 — 'I am the resurrection and the life') gives each moment ultimate seriousness; the Hindu cycle could be seen as reducing urgency since there are always future lives; Christian eternal life with a personal God (John 3:16) provides a relational, loving purpose that motivates ethical living; many Christians would argue resurrection in a transformed body is more meaningful than impersonal liberation. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4 or Bhagavad Gita 3.35 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which varnashrama dharma shapes a Hindu's daily life.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: varnashrama dharma specifies duties according to one's social role (varna) — for example a teacher (Brahmin varna) has specific duties of study and teaching; living within one's varna duties is seen as an act of devotion and karma-purification. Way 2: varnashrama dharma specifies duties according to life stage (ashrama) — a householder has duties of family, work and worship; a forest-dweller has duties of retreat and contemplation; these stages provide a structured spiritual path across a whole lifetime.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen in Mark's account of the calming of the storm (Mark 4:35-41).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete accurate point:
• A violent squall arose while Jesus and the disciples were crossing the Sea of Galilee.
• Jesus, who was asleep, woke up and commanded the wind and waves to be still — they obeyed immediately.
• The disciples were terrified and asked 'Who is this? Even the wind and the waves obey him!'

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen in Mark's account of the healing of Legion (Mark 5:1-20).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jesus met a man in the Gerasene region possessed by many demons who called themselves 'Legion'.
• Jesus commanded the demons out; they entered a herd of pigs that rushed into the lake and drowned.
• Afterwards the man was found sitting, clothed and in his right mind; the townspeople begged Jesus to leave.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the feeding of the five thousand (Mark 6:32-44) is important for Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per reason:
• The miracle shows Jesus's compassion for physical human need — he saw the crowd as 'sheep without a shepherd' and fed them, inspiring Christians to work for food justice and social care today.
• The actions of taking, blessing, breaking and giving bread echo the Last Supper and the Eucharist — this miracle points forward to the central Christian act of worship, giving it deep sacramental significance.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:21-43) shows who Jesus is.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point (one for the point, one for development), plus one mark for a named source:
• The miracle shows Jesus has power over death — he arrives after the girl has died, dismisses the mourners who laugh at him, and restores her to life with the command 'Talitha koum' (meaning 'Little girl, get up'), suggesting divine authority beyond ordinary human power.
• The miracle shows Jesus's compassion and personal care — he takes her hand, raises her gently, and tells her family to give her something to eat, showing a God who cares for individuals and their ordinary needs.
The fifth mark requires citing Mark 5:21-43 (or the Aramaic phrase 'Talitha koum' from the passage) as the source.

practice_questions.text:
'The miracles in Mark's Gospel prove that Jesus was the Son of God.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source; conclusion present.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few named sources.
Emerging (1-3): One-sided, minimal.

In support: The miracles show power over nature (storm, water), supply (feeding), evil (Legion) and death (Jairus's daughter) — all attributed in Jewish thought to God alone. The disciples' question 'Who is this?' implies the miracles are pointing to a divine identity. The feeding echoes Elijah and Moses, placing Jesus in the tradition of God's prophets.
Against: Humanists argue miracles can be scientifically explained or are literary/symbolic. Atheists argue the texts were written decades after Jesus and reflect the beliefs of the early Church rather than historical events. Even within Christianity, not all believers interpret the miracles as literal — some read them as powerful symbols of God's care and power rather than physical interventions.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the miracles in Mark's Gospel show Jesus's compassion.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• In the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus has compassion on the crowd 'because they were like sheep without a shepherd' (Mark 6:34) and provides for their physical hunger.
• In the healing of Legion (Mark 5:1-20), Jesus restores a deeply disturbed man who is living in isolation and pain — the result is dignity: 'sitting, clothed and in his right mind'.
• In the raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:21-43), Jesus responds immediately to a father's grief and takes the girl's hand gently, telling her family to give her something to eat.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Aquinas's cosmological argument for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete features: everything in motion was moved by something else — there must be an unmoved first mover (1); every effect has a cause — there must be a first uncaused cause (1); contingent things might not exist — there must be a necessary being (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Moses's experience at the burning bush (Exodus 3).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Moses encountered a bush that burned without being consumed (1); God spoke to Moses from the fire, calling him by name and revealing his identity (1); the experience transformed Moses and led him to a life-changing mission, suggesting it originated from a real divine source (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe answered prayer is evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Many Christians report specific outcomes that followed prayer — healing, guidance, provision — which they cannot explain except by God's action (2); 1 John 5:13-17 teaches that God hears those who ask according to his will, suggesting prayer involves real communication with a present and responsive God (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian reasons for believing the design argument supports the existence of God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The fine-tuning of the universe — physical constants are set so precisely that life would be impossible if they varied slightly — suggests intentional design by a creator (2); Romans 1:18-24 states that God's 'eternal power and divine nature' are 'clearly seen' in what has been made, providing scriptural support for the design argument (2); source credit for Romans 1:18-24 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Religious experience is the most convincing evidence that God exists.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: Exodus 3 (Moses), answered prayer (1 John 5:13-17), and the transforming effect of religious experience suggest genuine divine encounter. Counter: Dawkins argues experiences are brain-generated; Hume argues subjectivity means experiences provide no objective proof. Evaluate whether personal experience is stronger or weaker than philosophical arguments (design, cosmological). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: religious experience, cosmological, revelation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which atheist and Humanist arguments challenge the design argument, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per challenge; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution (On the Origin of Species, 1859) shows biological complexity arises through natural selection without requiring a designer — Dawkins calls this a 'blind watchmaker' (2); the existence of suffering and 'bad design' (vestigial organs, disease, extinction) suggests that if the universe was designed, the designer is not all-loving and all-powerful (2); source credit for naming Romans 1:18-24 in the Christian reply to these challenges (1). The source mark needs a religious source of wisdom and authority, so naming Darwin or Dawkins does not earn it.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which religious experience provides evidence for the existence of Allah in Islam.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: prophetic experience — Allah communicated directly with prophets such as Ibrahim, Musa and Muhammad (1); personal experiences of awe and spiritual transformation point to a reality beyond the human mind (1); Sufi practices of dhikr are designed to bring the practitioner into direct awareness of Allah's presence (1). Other valid Muslim perspectives accepted.

practice_questions.text: Outline three steps in al-Ghazali's kalam cosmological argument.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: everything that begins to exist has a cause (1); the universe began to exist (1); therefore the universe has a cause — a timeless, uncaused, powerful and personal being, identified as Allah (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims accept the kalam cosmological argument as evidence that Allah exists.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: everything that begins to exist has a cause, and Muslims hold that the universe began to exist, so it must have a cause outside itself — al-Ghazali identifies that cause as Allah (2); the first cause must be timeless, uncaused and immensely powerful, which matches the Muslim understanding of Allah as the eternal creator of everything (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim reasons for believing the design argument provides evidence for the existence of Allah, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Surah 2:164 lists natural signs (ayat) of Allah — the alternation of night and day, the water cycle, the winds and clouds — pointing to an intelligent creator (2); the precise fine-tuning of the universe's physical constants, which make life possible, suggests intentional design rather than random chance (2); source credit for Surah 2:164 named with surah number and verse range (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Al-Ghazali's kalam cosmological argument is the most convincing evidence that Allah exists.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Muslim case: al-Ghazali's kalam (Kitab al-Iqtisad) argues from the beginning of the universe to a first cause identified as Allah; modern cosmology (Big Bang) supports premise 2. Counter: atheists ask 'what caused Allah?'; question whether 'beginning to exist' applies to the universe as a whole; or whether the first cause need be personal. Evaluate: is kalam stronger than the design argument (Surah 2:164) or religious experience (Surah 2:118)? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: kalam, al-Ghazali, cosmological.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Sunni, Shi'a and Sufi Muslims differ in their approach to religious experience, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Sunni Muslims evaluate all personal religious experiences against the Qur'an and Sunnah — Surah 2:118 establishes that signs from Allah exist, but scholars use hadith scholarship to assess authenticity (2); Sufi Muslims seek direct transformative experience of Allah through devotional practices like dhikr (remembrance) and sama (devotional music), aiming for an inner knowledge of Allah that goes beyond doctrinal belief (2); source credit for Surah 2:118 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which a gurmukh Sikh expresses their God-centred life.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: regular Nam Japna (meditation on God's name); sewa (selfless service to others); attending the gurdwara and the sangat; living within the Sikh code of conduct (Rahit Maryada); kirat karni (honest work as service to God); overcoming haumai through the Guru's grace (GGS 226); sharing wealth and resources (vand chakna).

practice_questions.text: Outline three Sikh teachings about the equality of all people.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. GGS 349 says to recognise the Lord's light within all and not to judge people by social class or caste (1 mark). Sikhism therefore rejects the caste system as a denial of God's equal creation (1 mark). In practice this is shown through the langar (communal kitchen open to all) and shared worship in the sangat (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two forms of sewa and why they are important for Sikhs today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per form. Form 1: tan (physical sewa) — helping with practical tasks such as cleaning the gurdwara, serving langar, or caring for the sick; this is an act of devotion that helps overcome haumai by serving God in others. Form 2: dhan (service through wealth) — donating money or food for the benefit of the community; Guru Granth Sahib 26 affirms that service to God is expressed through service to humanity, making financial giving a spiritual act, not mere charity.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the sangat is important for Sikh religious life.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Reason 1: the sangat provides the community in which Nam Japna, sewa and worship are practised together — the collective experience of remembering God strengthens individual faith; without a sangat a Sikh is more vulnerable to haumai. Reason 2: the sangat enacts the Sikh teaching on equality — all members, regardless of caste, gender or background, gather as equals before the Guru Granth Sahib; the Sat Sangat is the ideal of a community genuinely focused on spiritual growth. 5th mark: ‘Guru Granth Sahib 1316 teaches that in the sangat God's name is reflected upon and his presence is felt.’

practice_questions.text:
'Sewa is more important than Nam Japna in Sikh religious life.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: sewa is the practical outworking of Sikh faith in the world; Guru Granth Sahib 26 identifies service as the expression of love for God; Mai Bhago exemplifies that active service (physical, even military) can be the highest form of Sikh devotion; the langar makes Sikh equality visible to the world; sewa addresses real human suffering in a concrete way. Arguments against: Nam Japna is listed first among the three core Sikh duties — meditating on God's name is the foundation from which all practice flows; Guru Granth Sahib 78 teaches that Nam Japna is the direct route to mukti; sewa motivated by ego (manmukh) is not genuine sewa — Nam Japna overcomes haumai, which is a prerequisite for genuine selfless service; the Mool Mantar opens with Ik Onkar (God is One) showing that the right relationship with God (through Nam Japna) is foundational. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least GGS 26 or GGS 1316 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Mai Bhago is significant for the Sikh teaching on equality.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: Mai Bhago led Sikh soldiers into battle when men had abandoned the Guru — this demonstrates that spiritual courage and leadership are not limited by gender; the spec names her as an example of women serving as leaders and teachers in Sikhism. Way 2: the Sikh Gurus affirmed the equality of women in worship and community life (Guru Granth Sahib 349) — Mai Bhago's story shows this equality expressed in action, not just in scripture; women can be full participants in both spiritual and practical (including military) aspects of Sikh life.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Aquinas's cosmological argument for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points from: everything in motion was put in motion by something else, so there must be an unmoved mover (1); everything has a cause, so there must be a first uncaused cause (1); contingent things could have not existed, so there must be a necessary being (1). Three distinct points required.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of William Paley's watchmaker analogy.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Paley argued that if you found a watch on a heath, its complexity would imply a watchmaker (1); he applied this to living organisms such as the eye, which are even more complex and purposeful than a watch (1); therefore the natural world must also have a designer — God (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Catholics use religious experience as evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Religious experiences produce lasting moral transformation and peace, suggesting they originate from God rather than the human mind alone (2); The Catechism (CCC 66-67) recognises that private revelations, though adding nothing to doctrine, can deepen faith and help believers live more fully by God's revelation (2). Other valid reasoning accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic reasons for believing the design argument supports belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The natural world shows clear evidence of order and purpose — eyes, ecosystems, physical constants — which is best explained by an intelligent creator rather than chance (2); Romans 1:18-24 explicitly states that God's eternal power and divine nature have been 'clearly seen' in the created world, lending scriptural support to the design argument (2); source credit for naming Romans 1:18-24 (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The cosmological argument is the most convincing proof of the existence of God.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing of arguments; justified conclusion. May argue the cosmological argument is strong because it begins from observable facts (not mere logic) and Aquinas's Three Ways are logically coherent, but evaluate whether it is more or less convincing than the design argument or religious experience; address Humanist and atheist rebuttals (infinite regress question, 'who made God' objection). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source, conclusion present but evaluative language limited. Developing (4-6): One side dominant, vague sources, descriptive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided, no sources. SPaG: cosmological, contingency, Aquinas, teleological.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue the design argument does not prove God exists, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution (On the Origin of Species, 1859) shows that complexity in living organisms arises through natural selection, not design — Dawkins argues this removes the need for a designer (2); the presence of suffering, disease and extinction in nature looks like poor design, making it hard to attribute the world to an all-loving, all-powerful God (2); source credit for naming Romans 1:18-24 in counter-argument framing, or naming Dawkins The Blind Watchmaker, or Darwin (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen during the Transfiguration of Jesus in Mark's Gospel (Mark 9:1-10).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Jesus's clothes became 'dazzling white, whiter than anyone in the world could bleach them.'
• Moses and Elias appeared and talked with Jesus.
• A voice from a cloud declared: 'This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!'

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen when Jesus and his disciples arrive at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27-33).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jesus asked the disciples who people said he was — they reported various views (John the Baptist, Elijah, a prophet).
• Peter declared: 'You are the Messiah.'
• Jesus predicted his own suffering and death; when Peter rebuked him, Jesus said 'Get behind me, Satan!'

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the conflicts of Jesus with the authorities in Mark's Gospel show what Jesus believed about himself.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• When Jesus healed the paralysed man (Mark 2:1-12) he first forgave his sins, claiming a power that belongs to God alone — the scribes were correct that 'only God can forgive sins', but Jesus's claim was that as Son of Man he possessed this divine authority.
• In the Sabbath controversies (Mark 2:23-3:6), Jesus called himself 'Lord of the Sabbath' — the Sabbath was established by God in the Torah, so claiming lordship over it was a claim to divine authority over the Law itself.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the cleansing of the Temple (Mark 11:15-18) is important in Mark's Gospel.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one mark for a named source:
• The Temple cleansing shows Jesus acting as a prophetic voice against corruption — by quoting Isaiah 56:7 ('My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations'), Jesus uses scripture to justify his action and claim that the Temple has become corrupted.
• The cleansing triggers the authorities' plot to kill Jesus — Mark 11:18 says 'the chief priests and teachers of the law began looking for a way to kill him', making it the moment that sets the passion narrative in motion.
The fifth mark requires citing Isaiah 56:7 or Jeremiah 7:11 as a named scriptural source Jesus quotes.

practice_questions.text:
'The messianic secret in Mark's Gospel shows that Jesus did not want to be recognised as the Messiah.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources and scholars; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Throughout Mark, Jesus commands silence after healings and miracles (e.g. after Jairus's daughter, after the healing of the leper). William Wrede argued the secrecy was Mark's theological invention to explain why Jesus was not widely recognised. Peter's well-meaning but misguided confession shows how dangerous the Messiah label was — it led immediately to misunderstanding about suffering.
Against: Jesus did not always silence people (the Gerasene demoniac was told to go and tell his family what God had done — Mark 5:19). The pattern may reflect Jesus's desire to control the terms of his mission rather than complete secrecy. At Peter's confession Jesus is not silent — he corrects, he predicts, he teaches. The Transfiguration suggests disclosure is coming but must wait until 'after the Son of Man has risen from the dead' (Mark 9:9).

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why the appearance of Moses and Elias at the Transfiguration is significant.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Moses represents the Law (Torah) — his presence shows Jesus is connected to and fulfils the Jewish Law.
• Elias (Elijah) represents the Prophets — in Jewish tradition, Elijah was expected to return before the Messiah came.
• Together, Moses and Elias signify that Jesus is the fulfilment of the whole of the Hebrew scriptures — Law and Prophets alike point to him.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Christians believe in the resurrection of the body after death.
- Christians believe in a final judgement where each person faces accountability for their earthly life.
- Christians believe in heaven — eternal life in God's presence.
- Christians believe in hell — eternal separation from God.
- Catholic (and some Orthodox) Christians believe in purgatory — purification for souls not yet fully holy.
- Protestant traditions (39 Articles) reject purgatory.
Each point must be identifiably distinct — not three sentences rephrasing the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Outline three teachings of the 39 Articles of Religion about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- The 39 Articles affirm belief in the resurrection of the body.
- They affirm eternal life in heaven for the saved.
- Article XXII explicitly rejects purgatory as 'a fond thing vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.'
- They reflect the Protestant (Anglican) position that heaven and hell are the only post-mortem destinations.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the problem of evil challenges Christian belief in God.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Moral evil (caused by human choices — war, murder, cruelty) challenges belief in an omnipotent God: if God is all-powerful, why does he allow humans to choose to harm each other? Some conclude that either God is not all-powerful, or he does not care.
- Natural evil (earthquakes, disease, floods) challenges belief in a benevolent God: unlike moral evil, natural evil cannot be blamed on human free will. A truly loving God could apparently design a world without natural disasters. Its existence seems incompatible with a creator who is both powerful and good.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian responses to the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- The free will defence (Augustine): God gave humans genuine freedom; moral evil is the result of that freedom being misused. God is not responsible for choices made by free creatures. A world with free will is better than a world of moral robots, even if free will is misused.
- The soul-making theodicy (Irenaeus, developed by John Hick in Evil and the God of Love, 1966): suffering is the necessary condition for moral and spiritual growth. The world is a 'vale of soul-making' — if everything were comfortable, humans would never develop courage, compassion or faith. Psalm 119 reflects this: 'It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees.'

The 5th mark: name a source — 'John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966)', 'Psalm 103', 'Psalm 119', '2 Corinthians 5:1-10', or the book of Job. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The vale of soul-making is the most convincing Christian response to the problem of evil.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources (Hick, Augustine, scripture); explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- The soul-making theodicy explains both moral and natural evil: both are necessary conditions for humans to develop virtues like courage, compassion and faith. It is more comprehensive than the free will defence, which only addresses moral evil.
- John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) grounds soul-making in Irenaeus's theology (c.130-202 CE) — the idea that humans are created immature and grow towards 'the likeness of God.' This gives the theodicy deep roots in Christian tradition, not just modern philosophy.
- The Bible supports the idea that suffering has a developmental purpose: Psalm 119 states 'It was good for me to be afflicted'; the book of Job ends not with an explanation of Job's suffering but with his deepened encounter with God.

Arguments against:
- The soul-making theodicy struggles with extreme suffering (Holocaust, childhood cancer) that goes far beyond any plausible 'educational' purpose. John Hick himself acknowledged this weakness. A child who dies in agony before developing moral character cannot easily be said to have 'benefited' from suffering.
- Augustine's free will defence has strong scriptural grounding in the Fall narrative (Genesis 3) and Paul's teaching on original sin. For many Christians this is more convincing because it identifies a cause of evil (human rebellion) rather than asking victims to find meaning in their pain.
- Non-religious critics argue that both theodicies are post-hoc rationalisations — invented to protect belief in God rather than genuine explanations. The problem of evil, they argue, gives good reason to conclude there is no God.
- Both theodicies leave natural evil partially unexplained. If God could have made a world without earthquakes or disease but chose not to, soul-making does not fully answer why.

SPaG: 'theodicy', 'eschatology', 'omnipotent', 'benevolent' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities between Christian and Islamic beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that after death all people will face judgement by God: Christians believe they will appear before 'the judgment seat of Christ' (2 Corinthians 5:10); Muslims believe their deeds will be weighed on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din).
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that the outcome of judgement is either heaven or hell: Christians describe heaven as eternal life in God's presence; Islamic teaching describes Paradise (Jannah) as a state of joy and divine favour. Both traditions describe hell as a place of punishment for the unrepentant.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim responses to the problem of suffering.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: life is a test (dunya as imtihaan) — suffering is part of Allah's purposeful trial (1); sabr (patient endurance) — trusting in Allah's wisdom and will (1); prayer and charity — addressing suffering practically through du'a, Zakah and sadaqah (1).

practice_questions.a: Up to 3 marks: Surah 1 (Al-Fatiha) praises Allah as Ar-Rahman (the Most Compassionate, universal mercy) (1); and as Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful, particular mercy for believers) (1); the surah is recited in every unit of Muslim prayer and sets the tone for how Muslims understand Allah's character — as fundamentally compassionate (1).
practice_questions.text: Outline three things Al-Fatiha (Surah 1) teaches about the nature of Allah.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Surah 1 (Al-Fatiha) praises Allah as Ar-Rahman (the Most Compassionate, universal mercy) (1); and as Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful, particular mercy for believers) (1); the surah is recited in every unit of Muslim prayer and establishes Allah's compassionate character as foundational (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the concept of sabr (patience) helps Muslims respond to suffering.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Sabr gives Muslims a spiritual framework for enduring hardship without despair — it involves active trust in Allah's wisdom rather than passive resignation, allowing the believer to maintain faith even in extreme suffering (2); Surah 2:153 links sabr to prayer: 'seek help through patience and prayer — Allah is with the patient' — suggesting that enduring with sabr brings the direct presence and support of Allah (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim responses to the problem of suffering, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per response; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Life as a test — Surah 2:155-157 explicitly teaches that Allah will test believers with fear, hunger and loss of goods and lives; those who respond with sabr and say 'to Allah we belong and to him we return' will receive glad tidings (2); charity — Surah 2:177 teaches that righteousness includes spending wealth on orphans, the needy and the wayfarer — Muslims address the conditions that produce suffering through obligatory Zakah and voluntary sadaqah (2); source credit for Surah 1 (Al-Fatiha), Surah 2:151-177, or a specific verse cited with surah number (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Suffering makes it impossible to believe that Allah is compassionate.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Case for the statement: the scale of suffering — famine, disease, the death of children — looks out of proportion to any purpose, and atheists and Humanists argue that a compassionate God would prevent it. Muslim case: Surah 1 names Allah as Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim; Surah 2:155-157 teaches that life is a test (dunya as imtihaan); Surah 2:153 promises that Allah is with the patient; Surah 2:177 makes charity a practical response. Evaluate whether the test framework answers the scale of the suffering. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, sources named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: sabr, Al-Fatiha, dunya.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which prayer and charity are practical Muslim responses to suffering, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per response; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Prayer (du'a) allows Muslims to bring their suffering directly to Allah, trusting he hears and will respond — Surah 2:153 teaches 'seek help through patience and prayer, for Allah is with the patient' (2); charity (Zakah and sadaqah) addresses the conditions that cause suffering — Surah 2:177 lists the needy, orphans and travellers as recipients of righteous giving, making charity a direct Qur'anic duty in response to poverty and hardship (2); source credit for Surah 2:153 or Surah 2:177 with verse numbers (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a Christian upbringing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete features: infant baptism or dedication (1); regular church attendance and involvement in the church community (1); prayer at home, including bedtime prayers and saying grace (1). Other valid features include Sunday school, faith schools, Christian festivals. Three distinct points required.

practice_questions.text: Outline three points Richard Dawkins makes in his argument that religious upbringing is indoctrination.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Dawkins argues there is no such thing as a 'Christian child' — only a child of Christian parents (1); he argues that labelling children with their parents' religion and teaching it before the child can evaluate it critically is a form of intellectual coercion (1); he claims in The God Delusion (2006) that this amounts to a form of harm to the child (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe religious upbringing may lead to genuine belief in God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Regular worship and prayer creates deep emotional and spiritual pathways from childhood that anchor faith through adult challenges, suggesting the belief is genuinely held rather than merely inherited (2); the fact that many adults who were raised as Christians continue in faith after having the opportunity to leave suggests the upbringing transmitted something real about God rather than just cultural habit (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian reasons for raising children in the faith, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Proverbs 22:6 ('Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it') teaches that early formation shapes lifelong character and faith — parents are commanded to provide this foundation (2); Christian community gives the child role models of lived faith, showing that belief is practised by real, trustworthy adults — this embodied witness is more powerful than abstract argument for a young person (2); source credit for Proverbs 22:6 named with chapter and verse (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Religious upbringing is the most important reason why people believe in God.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: Proverbs 22:6 supports the practice; upbringing creates genuine, lasting faith; millions of adults with a Christian upbringing freely choose to continue in faith. Counter: Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006) argues it is indoctrination before critical evaluation; many leave the faith; upbringing-based belief doesn't prove God exists — it only explains why people believe. Evaluate: is upbringing-based belief less 'genuine' than belief reached through argument? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: indoctrination, upbringing, Proverbs.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue religious upbringing may lead to a rejection of belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: If a child later encounters intellectual challenges to faith (such as the problem of evil) that their upbringing never addressed, they may conclude the beliefs were given without adequate reason and abandon them (2); Dawkins argues in The God Delusion (2006) that children raised in a faith before they can evaluate it critically have been denied the opportunity to reach their own informed conclusions, and some will eventually exercise that right by leaving (2); source credit for naming Proverbs 22:6 with chapter and verse (1). The source mark needs a religious source of wisdom and authority, so naming Dawkins does not earn it.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which suffering challenges Catholic belief in God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: if God is all-powerful he could prevent suffering (1); if God is all-loving he would want to prevent suffering (1); the existence of natural evil (earthquakes, disease) which humans did not cause makes it hard to attribute suffering to human free will alone (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Augustine's free-will defence.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Augustine argues evil is not a thing God created but the privation (absence) of good (1); evil entered the world through the Fall — humanity's free choice to disobey God (1); God gave humans free will because freely chosen love is more valuable than compelled love, but this freedom was misused (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Augustine's free-will defence and the Irenaean soul-making theodicy.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Augustine sees evil as the result of a fall from an original state of perfection — humans were created good but chose evil; Irenaeus sees humans as created immature and needing to develop, so suffering is part of the growth process rather than a consequence of a fall (2); Augustine's theodicy focuses on the origin of evil (the Fall) whereas Irenaeus (developed by Hick) focuses on the purpose of evil (moral development/soul-making) (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic responses to the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per response with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Prayer — Psalm 119 models the response of turning to God's word in suffering and trusting in his ultimate goodness even when circumstances suggest abandonment (2); Charity — Catholics address suffering practically, following Jesus's example and teachings such as Matthew 25:31-46 which calls Christians to care for the vulnerable (2); source credit for citing Psalm 119, Job, or another named biblical reference explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The soul-making theodicy gives a more convincing response to the problem of evil than Augustine's free-will defence.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; argument weighs both theodicies and responds to challenges; justified conclusion. May argue soul-making (Irenaeus/Hick) is stronger because it gives purpose to natural evil, not just moral evil, and addresses why God allows suffering rather than just where it came from. Counter: Augustine's privation argument is philosophically coherent and grounded in the Fall narrative; Hick's model faces the disproportionality problem (Holocaust). Both may be challenged as inadequate. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: theodicy, privation, Augustine, Irenaeus.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue that theodicies fail to solve the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Natural evil (disease, earthquakes) cannot easily be attributed to human free will — viruses do not choose to harm, making Augustine's free-will defence incomplete (2); the scale of suffering — including events like the Holocaust — seems vastly disproportionate to any developmental need, undermining the soul-making theodicy (2); source credit for Job (the Bible's most direct engagement with disproportionate suffering) or Psalm 119 cited explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Jewish public worship in the synagogue.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features. Acceptable: Torah readings and Haftarah (Prophets) readings; recitation of the Shema; the Amidah (Standing Prayer) recited by the congregation; a rabbi's sermon; communal minyan (quorum of ten); singing of hymns and psalms; prayers facing Jerusalem.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the Jewish food laws (kashrut).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features. Acceptable: kashrut divides food into kosher (permitted) and treifah (forbidden); Deuteronomy 14:3-10 forbids pigs and shellfish; permitted land animals chew the cud and have split hooves; meat and dairy must be kept apart; many kosher homes keep separate utensils and crockery for meat and dairy.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Shema is important for Jewish people today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason. Reason 1: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4 — 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one') is the foundational declaration of Jewish monotheism — reciting it twice daily keeps the belief in God's absolute oneness at the centre of daily life. Reason 2: the Shema is recited at the moment of death — making it both the daily affirmation and the final statement of faith; this gives it unique significance as a whole-life practice expressing the Jew's ultimate allegiance to the Almighty.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Jewish sacred texts shape the lives of Jewish people today.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: the Torah (part of the Tenakh) provides the 613 Mitzvot including kashrut and Shabbat that structure everyday life; Torah readings in synagogue every Shabbat and Monday/Thursday keep the text continuously present. Way 2: the Talmud (especially texts like Perkei Avot 2) provides practical ethical guidance for everyday situations that the Torah's broad principles do not directly address; it has shaped how Jews apply the Mitzvot in changing historical contexts. 5th mark: ‘Perkei Avot 2 teaches that all work should be done with Torah as its foundation.’

practice_questions.text:
'The Shema is more important than the Amidah in Jewish worship.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the most fundamental declaration of Jewish monotheism and the defining statement of Jewish faith; it is recited at the critical moments of life and death; the Mezuzah ensures it is physically present in every Jewish home; it is the first prayer taught to Jewish children. Arguments against: the Amidah (nineteen blessings) is the central prayer of every Jewish service — it is obligatory at every shacharit, mincha and maariv; it covers praise, petition and thanksgiving in a comprehensive way; some rabbinic opinion holds that the Amidah is the most important prayer because it constitutes the formal 'service of the heart'; both are essential and the comparison is partly artificial. Secure (7-9): Both sides; Deuteronomy 6:4 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Orthodox and Reform Jewish approaches to kashrut.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference. Difference 1: Orthodox Jews regard kashrut as a divine commandment derived directly from Deuteronomy 14:3-10 and the Talmud — they observe it strictly at home and outside, including only eating in certified kosher establishments; Reform Jews may observe kashrut selectively as a matter of Jewish identity rather than divine obligation. Difference 2: Orthodox Jews maintain strict separation of meat and dairy (separate utensils, pots, waiting periods between eating meat and dairy); many Reform Jews observe this only partially or not at all, since they see the Oral Torah as tradition open to re-evaluation rather than divinely binding law.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of liturgical Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Liturgical worship follows a fixed, formal structure (set prayers, set responses).
- It is used by Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
- The Book of Common Prayer (Anglican) or Roman Rite (Catholic) provides the set texts.
- A minister or priest leads the congregation through the set order.
- The Eucharist/Mass is typically central to liturgical worship.
Do not award marks for three sentences that elaborate the same point.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between Pentecostal and Anglican worship.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Pentecostal worship is spontaneous and led by the Holy Spirit; there is no fixed order of service or prayer book.
- It may include speaking in tongues (glossolalia), prophecy, healing prayer and contemporary music with guitars and clapping.
- Anglican worship is liturgical — following the set structure of the Book of Common Prayer or Common Worship, with set prayers and responses led by a minister.
[1 mark per accurate contrasting point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian beliefs about sacraments differ between denominations.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Catholics and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments; most Protestant traditions (including Anglicans, as stated in the 39 Articles XXV) recognise only two — baptism and the Eucharist. Protestants reduced the number because only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus in the Gospels; the five Catholic sacraments are described in the 39 Articles as not being 'Sacraments of the Gospel.'
- The meaning of the Eucharist differs significantly: Catholics teach transubstantiation — the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ (the outward appearance remains but the substance changes). Most Protestant Christians hold either a memorialist view (bread and wine are symbols only) or a spiritual presence view (Christ is spiritually but not physically present). This is one of the most significant points of division in the Reformation.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians use set prayers, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Set prayers connect Christians to centuries of tradition and unite believers across denominations: the Lord's Prayer is said in virtually all Christian services worldwide, from Catholic Mass to Baptist Sunday worship. Matthew 6:9-13 records Jesus specifically teaching this prayer to his disciples as a model — its regular use keeps Christians grounded in the pattern Jesus himself gave.
- Set prayers provide a reliable structure for worship, especially for those who struggle to find words: the Book of Common Prayer gives worshippers tested, beautiful language for confession, thanksgiving and praise. Using the same words as Christians across generations creates a sense of continuity with the historic Church.

The 5th mark: name a specific source — 'Matthew 6:9-13 (the Lord's Prayer)', 'the Book of Common Prayer' or another clearly identified text. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Liturgical worship is more important than informal worship for Christians today.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- Liturgical worship connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides a shared structure that unites the Church globally: the same Eucharistic prayers, the same Lord's Prayer, the same lectionary readings unite Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox across the world. The Book of Common Prayer has shaped English-speaking Christianity for over 350 years.
- Liturgical worship is ordered and biblical: set scripture readings, the Nicene Creed and the Lord's Prayer ensure that core doctrine and key texts are rehearsed regularly. This guards against theological drift and ensures worshippers are formed by the whole of Scripture, not just a preacher's preferences.
- Sacraments (central to liturgical worship) are considered by Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican Christians to be genuine channels of God's grace — not symbolic but effective. Without sacramental worship, Christians may miss out on the grace God intends to give through these means.

Arguments against:
- Pentecostal and charismatic worship has grown fastest globally, suggesting that many Christians find less structured, Spirit-led worship more meaningful and life-giving. Jesus himself warned against empty, repetitive prayer (Matthew 6:7 — 'do not keep on babbling'); liturgical services can become mechanical.
- Informal prayer allows Christians to bring their personal concerns before God in their own words: Jesus encouraged private, personal prayer in Matthew 6:6 ('go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen'). Formal liturgy cannot always meet the individual's specific spiritual needs.
- Many Baptist, Methodist and evangelical Christians argue that the New Testament church was not liturgical in the Catholic sense: the emphasis in the early Church was on preaching, communal prayer and breaking of bread in simple settings, not an elaborate ritual structure.

SPaG: 'liturgical', 'Eucharist', 'sacrament', 'Pentecostal' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Protestant and Catholic approaches to baptism.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The timing of baptism differs: Catholics (and Anglicans, Orthodox) practise infant baptism (paedo-baptism), baptising babies into the community of faith, believing it removes original sin and incorporates the child into the Body of Christ. Baptists and many evangelicals practise believer's baptism — only those who have personally declared faith in Jesus are baptised, because it is seen as a public expression of individual faith.
- The theological meaning differs: in Catholic theology, baptism is a sacrament that confers grace, washes away original sin and makes the person a member of the Church. In Baptist theology, baptism is an ordinance — an act of obedience that publicly expresses a faith already present in the believer's heart. Grace is received through faith, not through the water of baptism.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a gurdwara and their significance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features with brief significance. Acceptable: takht (raised throne on which the Guru Granth Sahib rests, showing its status as eternal Guru); chanani (canopy over the GGS, a mark of royal honour and respect); chaur (fan waved over the GGS, sign of reverence); Nishan Sahib (orange/blue flag outside, marks the gurdwara's presence); four doors (open on all sides to all people, embodying Sikh equality); langar hall (communal kitchen serving free food to all).

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why the langar is important for Sikhs today.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Langar is the free communal meal served in every gurdwara to all visitors regardless of background (1 mark). It expresses sewa (selfless service) — GGS 967 teaches that sharing with others is devotion (1 mark). It embodies Sikh equality: all sit on the floor at the same level, dissolving caste and social distinctions in the Guru's presence (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Nam Japna is important for Sikh religious life.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: Nam Japna (GGS 1142) dissolves haumai (ego) — through repeated meditation on God's name the mind becomes purified and the soul moves toward mukti; it is the practical means by which a gurmukh Sikh overcomes the self-centredness of the manmukh. Way 2: Nam Japna is practised both individually (silent meditation, personal prayer) and communally (kirtan — singing hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib), binding the Sikh community in shared devotion and structuring both the individual's day and the congregation's worship.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two differences between Sikh and Christian worship.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Difference 1: Sikh prayer (Nam Japna) is primarily meditative repetition of God's name ('Waheguru') to purify the mind and dissolve ego; Christian prayer (Lord's Prayer) is primarily addressed to a personal God in words of praise, petition and confession. Difference 2: Sikh worship centres on the Guru Granth Sahib as the living eternal Guru; Christian worship in the Mass (Catholic) or liturgical service centres on the Bible reading and, for Catholics, the Eucharist as Christ's real presence. 5th mark: ‘Guru Granth Sahib 305 teaches that a Sikh of the Guru rises in the early morning to meditate on God's name’ or cite Matthew 6:9-13 for the Lord's Prayer.

practice_questions.text:
'The gurdwara is the most important institution in Sikh religious life.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the gurdwara is where the Guru Granth Sahib (eternal Guru) is present and treated as a living reality; all major Sikh ceremonies (Amrit Sanskar, Naam Karan, Akhand Path) take place there; the langar (GGS 967) makes equality visible and feeds the community; the four doors embody Sikh teaching on equality; Guru Granth Sahib 1391 affirms it as open to all. Arguments against: the Guru Granth Sahib itself, not the building, is the eternal Guru — Sikh worship and Nam Japna can take place at home; the sangat can meet wherever Sikhs gather; the three core duties (Nam Japna, kirat karni, vand chakna) can be practised without a gurdwara; for Sikhs living as a minority without a nearby gurdwara, home devotion and the Nitnem maintain the gurmukh life. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least GGS 1391 or GGS 967 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) is important to Sikhs worldwide.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: it is the most sacred gurdwara in Sikhism, a global centre of pilgrimage and spiritual significance; it was founded by Guru Arjan Dev and the Guru Granth Sahib is present continuously; the four doors embody Sikh equality (open to all); it is surrounded by the sacred pool (Amrit Sarovar); tens of thousands of langar meals are served daily; it is the architectural and spiritual heart of Sikhism.

practice_questions.text: Outline three forms of Hindu worship.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three named and briefly described forms. Acceptable: puja (ritual offering of flowers, food, water, incense to deity); havan (sacred fire sacrifice); darshan (auspicious sight of the deity); arti (waving of oil lamps before deity); bhajan (devotional songs); kirtan (communal chanting); japa (repetition of God's name).

practice_questions.text: Describe the Hindu cosmological concept of maya.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Maya is the power of illusion that causes beings to mistake the phenomenal world for ultimate reality (1 mark); it conceals the true nature of Brahman from ordinary perception (1 mark); overcoming maya through jnana yoga (wisdom) or bhakti (devotion) is central to achieving liberation/moksha (1 mark); maya works alongside prakriti (matter) and the tri-guna, the three qualities that make up the material world (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two of the four forms of yoga and how they lead to liberation in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per form. Karma yoga: selfless action performed without attachment to results as an offering to God (Bhagavad Gita 6.44-47); this purifies karma without generating new bondage, gradually moving the atman toward liberation. Bhakti yoga: the path of loving devotion to a personal deity (Bhagavad Gita 9.13-27); even simple offerings made with pure devotion are accepted by Krishna, making this path widely accessible and central to popular Hinduism.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Hindu teachings about how to respond to suffering.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Teaching 1: ahimsa (non-violence) — responding to suffering with compassion and non-harm toward all living beings; the highest dharma is not to harm any being. Teaching 2: yoga as active spiritual response — karma yoga allows Hindus to act ethically in the world without generating fresh karma-bondage; bhakti yoga channels suffering into devotion to God, transforming pain into spiritual growth. 5th mark: ‘The Mahabharata 5.39 teaches that the highest dharma is not to harm any living being.’

practice_questions.text:
'Bhakti yoga is the most important of the four paths to liberation in Hinduism.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Bhagavad Gita 9.13-27 shows Krishna personally affirming that devotion in any form — even a leaf or flower — is accepted, making bhakti accessible to all regardless of social position; it engages the heart as well as the intellect; it is the most widely practised path in popular Hinduism; bhakti saints (Mirabai, Tukaram) show its transformative power. Arguments against: the Bhagavad Gita presents all four paths as valid routes to the same goal; jnana yoga directly addresses maya (illusion) which is the root of all suffering; karma yoga is the path of righteous action in the world and may be seen as most immediately relevant to everyday life; raja yoga (Bhagavad Gita 6.20-31) cultivates the perfectly still mind that directly perceives Brahman. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least one Bhagavad Gita passage named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Hindu teachings about the yugas (ages of the universe).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: there are four yugas — Satya, Treta, Dvapara and Kali; Satya Yuga is the golden age of truth and righteousness; Kali Yuga is the current age, described in the Mahabharata as a time of moral decline and spiritual degeneration; the yugas together form a Mahayuga, and many Mahayugas form a cosmic cycle; the cycle of yugas reflects Hindu cosmology's cyclical rather than linear view of time; Rig Veda 10.129 reflects on the mystery of creation before the cosmos began.

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the seven Catholic sacraments.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete sacraments named, e.g. Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist. Each must be a separately identifiable sacrament. Bonus understanding of purpose counts if offered but three named items are required.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about the Mass.
practice_questions.marks: May include: the Eucharist is the 'source and summit' of Catholic life (Lumen Gentium 7); the Mass has two main parts (Liturgy of the Word and Liturgy of the Eucharist); Catholics believe bread and wine become Christ's body and blood (transubstantiation); the Mass makes present again the sacrifice of Calvary. Three accurate relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways Catholics use popular piety in their worship.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations required. E.g. (1) The Rosary — a meditative prayer using beads, combining set prayers with meditation on the mysteries of Christ's life; it deepens devotion to Mary and keeps Catholics focused on the Gospel. (2) Stations of the Cross — fourteen pictorial stations depicting Christ's passion; moving through them in prayer allows Catholics to enter imaginatively into Christ's suffering, especially during Lent. Development beyond naming the practice required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic beliefs about the Eucharist, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) The Eucharist is the 'source and summit' of Catholic life — Lumen Gentium paragraph 7 teaches that all Catholic worship flows from and leads back to the Mass; (2) At the consecration, bread and wine become Christ's body and blood (transubstantiation) — rooted in Jesus' words at the Last Supper. 5th mark requires a named source: Lumen Gentium 7, or CCC 1210–1211.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between Catholic liturgical worship and evangelical non-liturgical worship.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete contrasts, e.g. (1) Catholic Mass follows a fixed structure; evangelical worship is flexible and spontaneous; (2) The Eucharist is central to Catholic worship; preaching is often central to evangelical worship; (3) Catholic worship is led by an ordained priest; evangelical worship may be led by any believer gifted by the Spirit.

practice_questions.text: 'The Eucharist is more important than any other form of Catholic worship.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; weighs explicitly; justified conclusion. FOR: Lumen Gentium 7 calls it 'source and summit' — Catholics attend Mass every Sunday as an obligation; transubstantiation means it is a direct encounter with Christ himself; all other sacraments flow from and lead to it. AGAINST: prayer (including the Rosary and Eucharistic adoration) may be more accessible daily; some argue that service to the poor (Matthew 25:31–46) is the most important expression of Catholic faith; others value popular piety for making faith personal. Named sources: Lumen Gentium 7; CCC 1210–1211; Matthew 6:5–14. Secure (7–9): both sides, at least one source. Developing (4–6): one-sided. Emerging (1–3): minimal.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that the Qur'an teaches about justice in Surah An-Nisa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Surah 4:135 commands Muslims to stand firmly for justice even against themselves, their parents or their relatives.
• Justice must be impartial — it should not favour the rich over the poor or the powerful over the weak.
• Justice is grounded in Allah's own character as Al-'Adl (the Just) — because Allah is just, humans are required to be just as his stewards on earth.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that Muslims believe about shirk.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Shirk means associating partners with Allah — giving to any created thing the worship or ultimate loyalty that belongs to Allah alone.
• It is the opposite of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and is considered the one sin that cannot be forgiven if persisted in until death.
• The Qur'an condemns idolatry as a form of shirk — Surah 7:148-150 illustrates this with the golden calf story.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Shari'ah law is important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Shari'ah provides a comprehensive guide to worship and personal conduct — daily prayer, fasting, halal food laws and zakah are all part of Shari'ah, giving Muslim life a coherent, God-centred structure that goes beyond merely following human custom.
• Shari'ah provides a framework for justice and ethics — its principles of fairness, care for the vulnerable and prohibition of exploitation are applied in Muslim communities around the world, whether in full legal systems or in personal ethical choices.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the teaching about shirk shapes how Muslims live today.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Shirk shapes Muslim worship: because ascribing partners to Allah is forbidden, all prayer and devotion must be directed to Allah alone — no image, statue or mediating figure can be the object of worship. This is why mosques are adorned with geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than images of Allah or the prophets.
• Shirk shapes Muslim responses to other religions: Islam's insistence on Tawhid means Muslims cannot accept Trinitarian Christianity or Hindu polytheism as fully valid, though they recognise the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) as having received earlier revelation from Allah.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 7:148-150 (golden calf) or another shirk-related passage as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Following Shari'ah law is unnecessary for Muslims living in modern Britain.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support (of the statement): Humanists argue that ethics should be based on human reason and democratic consent, not divine commands. Some Shari'ah rulings developed in 7th-century Arabia may not be appropriate for 21st-century Britain. Muslims in Britain live under civil law, which already provides frameworks for justice and rights. Following Shari'ah in all details would create two parallel legal systems.
Against: The Qur'an commands obedience to Allah and the Messenger (Surah 4:59) — for committed Muslims, Shari'ah is not optional but an expression of submission to Allah. Even in Britain, Muslims observe many aspects of Shari'ah (prayer times, halal food, fasting, family law in some cases). Many Muslim scholars argue Shari'ah's principles of justice, compassion and care for the vulnerable are entirely compatible with modern life. The Sunnah (Surah 33:21-36) provides the model for how Shari'ah is lived — adaptable to context while rooted in divine guidance.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the golden calf story in Surah 7:148-150 illustrates the problem of shirk.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• The Israelites made and worshipped a physical image in Moses's absence — this substituted a visible, created thing for the invisible, eternal God.
• The calf could not speak, guide or help its worshippers — this shows the Qur'an's argument that idols are powerless compared to Allah.
• Moses's anger on his return demonstrates how seriously shirk is treated — it is a betrayal of the covenant relationship with Allah.

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the Five Precepts (pancha sila) in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three of: abstain from killing living beings; abstain from taking what is not given; abstain from sexual misconduct; abstain from false speech; abstain from intoxicants.

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the Five Khandas (aggregates) in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three of: form (rupa); sensation (vedana); perception (sanna); mental formations (sankhara); consciousness (vinnana). Naming the aggregate earns the mark. The Khandha Sutta teaches that none of them is a permanent self.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between the Arahant ideal in Theravada Buddhism and the Bodhisattva ideal in Mahayana Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference.
