Difference 1: an Arahant achieves individual liberation (nibbana) and will not be reborn; a Bodhisattva delays personal nibbana to liberate all sentient beings. Difference 2: the Arahant follows the Four Noble Truths primarily for personal liberation; the Bodhisattva develops the six perfections (paramitas) over many lifetimes out of compassion for others.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Buddhist teachings about kamma.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks for two developed explanations, +1 for naming Dhammapada 181-187 or the Khuddakapatha. Teaching 1: intentional actions (physical, verbal, mental) have consequences that shape future experience and rebirth — good actions generate merit that leads toward liberation. Teaching 2: kamma is linked to the cycle of samsara — harmful actions produce unfavourable rebirths; understanding kamma motivates Buddhists to practise the Five Precepts. 5th mark: ‘Dhammapada 181-187 teaches that merit (punya) accumulated through good actions brings positive outcomes’ or ‘The Khuddakapatha teaches that merit built up by good actions is a treasure that stays with a person.’

practice_questions.text:
'Meditation is more important than ethics for a Buddhist's spiritual development.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; weighs perspectives; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: meditation directly leads to nibbana through insight into the Three Marks; vipassana is the method by which the Buddha himself achieved enlightenment; samatha and metta bhavana transform the mind at its root; the Amitayus Meditation Sutra shows that visualisation of the Buddha through meditation can achieve rebirth in the Pure Land. Arguments against: ethics (sila) is the foundation without which meditation cannot develop — the Threefold Way puts sila first; the Five Precepts and kamma are part of daily life for all Buddhists, not just meditators; the Dhammapada 1-2 states that mind leads all actions, and ethical action precedes and enables meditative practice; for Mahayana Buddhists, the Six Perfections include generosity and ethics alongside meditation. Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one text named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two types of Buddhist meditation and how they are practised.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per type (1 for identification, 2 for developed description of practice). Type 1: samatha — concentration meditation; the practitioner focuses attention on a single object (e.g. the breath) until the mind becomes calm and stable; this is the foundation for deeper practice. Type 2: vipassana — insight meditation; using the stable mind developed through samatha, the practitioner directly observes the arising and passing of physical and mental experience, perceiving anicca, dukkha and anatta in direct experience.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a Buddhist vihara.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate features. Acceptable: shrine room (with buddharupa as focus); meditation hall (for communal practice); library (reflecting importance of wisdom and learning, as in Kimsila Sutta); monks' quarters; image of the Buddha; incense and candles; facing east.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen during puja in a Buddhist vihara.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate points. Acceptable: prostrations before the buddharupa; offering flowers, incense and candles or lamps; chanting suttas such as the Mangala Sutta; taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Buddhist festivals are important for Buddhists today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: Wesak provides an annual opportunity for lay Buddhists to deepen practice, make offerings and remember the Buddha’s enlightenment — it reinforces the community and motivates commitment to the path. Way 2: Vassa (Rain Retreat) provides a structured intensive period of monastic practice tied to the Anapanasati Sutta; the Kathina ceremony that follows strengthens the lay-monastic relationship through merit-making.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Buddhist places of worship support Buddhist practice.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: the shrine room with buddharupa helps Buddhists focus their minds on the Buddha’s qualities; the Vakkali Sutta explains that seeing the Dhamma is seeing the Buddha — the image points to the truth. Way 2: the library in the vihara supports the development of wisdom (panna), which the Kimsila Sutta describes as one of the marks of good conduct when visiting a monastery. 5th mark: name either the Vakkali Sutta or the Kimsila Sutta explicitly.

practice_questions.text:
'Buddhist puja is no different from Christian worship.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; conclusion with justified position. Arguments in support (similarities): both involve communal gathering in a dedicated space; both use physical objects and actions to express devotion; both aim to strengthen commitment to spiritual practice; both have regular days of observance. Arguments against (differences): Buddhist puja does not address an omnipotent creator God — it expresses reverence for the Buddha’s qualities and cultivates the practitioner’s own mind (Vakkali Sutta); Christian worship, whether liturgical (Lord’s Prayer, Matthew 6:9-13) or charismatic, involves direct communication with a personal God who is other than the worshipper; the buddharupa is not regarded as containing divine presence in the way Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the Eucharist. Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Very brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen during the Tibetan Buddhist death ritual.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three separate points. Acceptable: the Tibetan Book of the Dead is read to the dying or deceased; the text guides consciousness through the bardo (intermediate state between death and rebirth); the consciousness is instructed to recognise the clear light of reality; relatives and monks may chant and pray; cremation typically follows; the process reflects belief in rebirth and liberation through recognition of reality.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why Christians go on pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) To deepen faith by visiting the places where Jesus lived and died (Jerusalem); (2) For spiritual renewal and community (Iona, Taize); (3) As an act of penance, thanksgiving or seeking healing (Walsingham, Lourdes). Three separately identifiable reasons.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Christians remember during Holy Week.
practice_questions.marks: May include: Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem); Maundy Thursday (Last Supper, foot washing); Good Friday (crucifixion and death of Jesus); Holy Saturday (waiting); Easter Sunday (resurrection celebrated). Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the local church serves its community.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Outreach work — local churches run food banks, debt counselling and community cafes, meeting practical needs in their area and putting Matthew 25 into practice; (2) Ecumenical partnership — local churches of different denominations work together on shared projects, expressing the prayer of Jesus for unity in John 17:21. Development required beyond naming the activity.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Easter is the most important Christian festival, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Easter celebrates the resurrection, which Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:17 calls the basis of all Christian faith — 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile'; (2) Easter marks the defeat of sin and death — it is the moment when Christ's atoning work on the cross is vindicated, giving Christians hope of their own resurrection. 5th mark requires a named source: 1 Corinthians 15:12–34.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between pilgrimage to Iona and pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points: (1) Jerusalem is the site of Jesus' death and resurrection — the most historically significant Christian site; Iona is a site of Celtic spirituality and social justice without direct gospel-history significance; (2) Jerusalem is shared by Christians, Jews and Muslims and has geopolitical complexity; Iona is a quieter, retreat-focused community site; (3) Jerusalem pilgrimage is ancient; Iona Community was founded in 1938 by George MacLeod.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important work of the worldwide Church is evangelism.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed, named sources, explicit weighing, justified conclusion. FOR: the Great Commission (Mark 16:9–20) instructs disciples to 'go into all the world and proclaim the good news'; 1 Corinthians 15 shows the resurrection must be proclaimed; without evangelism the Church shrinks and cannot fulfil its purpose. AGAINST: Matthew 25:31–46 teaches that serving 'the least of these' is serving Christ — development work (Christian Aid) is equally central; actions speak louder than words; some argue that justice and reconciliation are the primary mission. Named sources: Mark 16:9–20; 1 Corinthians 15; Matthew 25:31–46. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of liturgical Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Liturgical worship follows a fixed, formal structure (set prayers, set responses).
- It is used by Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
- The Book of Common Prayer (Anglican) or Roman Rite (Catholic) provides the set texts.
- A minister or priest leads the congregation through the set order.
- The Eucharist/Mass is typically central to liturgical worship.
Do not award marks for three sentences that elaborate the same point.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between Pentecostal worship and Anglican worship.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Pentecostal worship is spontaneous and led by the Holy Spirit; there is no fixed order of service or prayer book.
- It may include speaking in tongues (glossolalia), prophecy, healing prayer and contemporary music with guitars and clapping.
- Anglican worship is liturgical — following the set structure of the Book of Common Prayer or Common Worship, with set prayers and responses led by a minister.
[1 mark per accurate contrasting point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian beliefs about sacraments differ between denominations.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Catholics and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments; most Protestant traditions (including Anglicans, as stated in the 39 Articles XXV) recognise only two — baptism and the Eucharist. Protestants reduced the number because only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus in the Gospels; the five Catholic sacraments are described in the 39 Articles as not being 'Sacraments of the Gospel.'
- The meaning of the Eucharist differs significantly: Catholics teach transubstantiation — the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ (the outward appearance remains but the substance changes). Most Protestant Christians hold either a memorialist view (bread and wine are symbols only) or a spiritual presence view (Christ is spiritually but not physically present). This is one of the most significant points of division in the Reformation.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians use set prayers, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Set prayers connect Christians to centuries of tradition and unite believers across denominations: the Lord's Prayer is said in virtually all Christian services worldwide, from Catholic Mass to Baptist Sunday worship. Matthew 6:9-13 records Jesus specifically teaching this prayer to his disciples as a model — its regular use keeps Christians grounded in the pattern Jesus himself gave.
- Set prayers provide a reliable structure for worship, especially for those who struggle to find words: the Book of Common Prayer gives worshippers tested, beautiful language for confession, thanksgiving and praise. Using the same words as Christians across generations creates a sense of continuity with the historic Church.

The 5th mark: name a specific source — 'Matthew 6:9-13 (the Lord's Prayer)', 'the Book of Common Prayer' or another clearly identified text. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Liturgical worship is more important than informal worship for Christians today.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- Liturgical worship connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides a shared structure that unites the Church globally: the same Eucharistic prayers, the same Lord's Prayer, the same lectionary readings unite Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox across the world. The Book of Common Prayer has shaped English-speaking Christianity for over 350 years.
- Liturgical worship is ordered and biblical: set scripture readings, the Nicene Creed and the Lord's Prayer ensure that core doctrine and key texts are rehearsed regularly. This guards against theological drift and ensures worshippers are formed by the whole of Scripture, not just a preacher's preferences.
- Sacraments (central to liturgical worship) are considered by Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican Christians to be genuine channels of God's grace — not symbolic but effective. Without sacramental worship, Christians may miss out on the grace God intends to give through these means.

Arguments against:
- Pentecostal and charismatic worship has grown fastest globally, suggesting that many Christians find less structured, Spirit-led worship more meaningful and life-giving. Jesus himself warned against empty, repetitive prayer (Matthew 6:7 — 'do not keep on babbling'); liturgical services can become mechanical.
- Informal prayer allows Christians to bring their personal concerns before God in their own words: Jesus encouraged private, personal prayer in Matthew 6:6 ('go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen'). Formal liturgy cannot always meet the individual's specific spiritual needs.
- Many Baptist, Methodist and evangelical Christians argue that the New Testament church was not liturgical in the Catholic sense: the emphasis in the early Church was on preaching, communal prayer and breaking of bread in simple settings, not an elaborate ritual structure.

SPaG: 'liturgical', 'Eucharist', 'sacrament', 'Pentecostal' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Protestant and Catholic approaches to baptism.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The timing of baptism differs: Catholics (and Anglicans, Orthodox) practise infant baptism (paedo-baptism), baptising babies into the community of faith, believing it removes original sin and incorporates the child into the Body of Christ. Baptists and many evangelicals practise believer's baptism — only those who have personally declared faith in Jesus are baptised, because it is seen as a public expression of individual faith.
- The theological meaning differs: in Catholic theology, baptism is a sacrament that confers grace, washes away original sin and makes the person a member of the Church. In Baptist theology, baptism is an ordinance — an act of obedience that publicly expresses a faith already present in the believer's heart. Grace is received through faith, not through the water of baptism.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about the purpose of marriage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: procreation — bringing children into the world and raising them in the faith (1); companionship and emotional fulfilment between spouses (1); strengthening the ummah — the worldwide Muslim community is built through faithful families (1). Other valid purposes accepted.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the ummah supports Muslim families.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the mosque community provides rites of passage (Aqiqah, nikah ceremonies, funeral prayers) (1); madrasah (Islamic school) provides religious education for children (1); Zakah and sadaqah provide financial support for those in need within the community (1). Other valid support mechanisms accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims believe sexual relationships should only take place within marriage.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Surah 23:5-11 teaches that believers 'guard their private parts' except within marriage — sex outside this framework is regarded as transgressing divinely set limits, which Muslims believe leads to individual and social harm (2); marriage provides the committed, legally binding context in which children can be raised securely — ensuring procreation takes place within a stable family unit as Allah intended (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim teachings about the purpose of the family, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Surah 46:15-18 teaches that children must honour their parents and care for them as they age — the family is the unit of mutual obligation across generations, not just between parents and young children (2); Surah 3:102-105 calls the ummah to hold fast to Allah's rope and not be divided — families are strengthened by embedding them in the mosque community, which provides mutual support (2); source credit for Surah 4, Surah 46:15-18, or Surah 3:102-105 named with verse numbers (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Muslim teaching on marriage is too restrictive for the 21st century.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Counter case: Humanists argue consensual relationships have equal value without marriage; same-sex relationships are excluded by classical jurisprudence; cohabitation is a normal feature of modern society. Muslim case: Surah 4, Surah 23:5-11 — marriage provides security, procreation within a committed framework, and reflects divine guidance that transcends shifting social norms; ummah support (Surah 3:102-105) shows the communal context. Evaluate: is the 'too restrictive' charge based on assuming a particular cultural standard as the norm? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: nikah, ummah, procreation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Sunni and Shi'a Islam differ in their understanding of marriage, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Shi'a Muslims (particularly Twelver Shi'as) permit temporary marriage (mut'ah) for a specified period, while Sunni Muslims regard this as forbidden on the basis that the Prophet abolished it — this is a significant point of divergence in Islamic marriage law (2); all four Sunni schools and Shi'a jurisprudence agree that the nikah contract requires the free consent of both parties — Surah 4 provides the Qur'anic framework for marriage rights and responsibilities that both traditions draw on (2); source credit for Surah 4 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why Catholics go on pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete reasons, e.g. (1) To seek healing or miracle (e.g. at Lourdes); (2) As an act of penance or devotion; (3) To connect with the historical sites of Jesus' life and death (e.g. Jerusalem). Each must be a separately identifiable reason.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the work of CAFOD.
practice_questions.marks: May include: CAFOD is the Catholic development charity for England and Wales; it works in partnership with local communities in the Global South; it does long-term development and emergency relief; it is motivated by Matthew 25:31–46 (the Sheep and Goats); it puts Catholic Social Teaching into practice. Three accurate relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two purposes of the Catholic funeral rite.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) The funeral rite maintains communion with the deceased — prayers are offered for their purification in purgatory, and the Funeral Mass applies the merits of Christ's sacrifice on their behalf; (2) The rite proclaims the resurrection — by gathering the community to celebrate the Eucharist at a funeral, the Church publicly announces its belief in eternal life, giving hope to mourners. Development beyond bare statements required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways Catholic Social Teaching is put into practice, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Through CAFOD — the agency carries out development work among the poorest, motivated by Evangelii Gaudium's call to include the poor (paragraphs 182–237); (2) Through individual Catholics visiting the sick, homeless or imprisoned, following Matthew 25:31–46 in which Jesus identifies himself with 'the least of these.' The 5th mark requires a named source — Evangelii Gaudium paragraphs 182–237, or Matthew 25:31–46.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between how Catholics and Protestants view pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) Catholics believe pilgrimage earns spiritual merit; many Protestants reject this; (2) Catholics have official sites (Lourdes, Rome) with Catechism recognition; many Protestants have no equivalent tradition; (3) Catholic pilgrimage often involves Marian shrines; most Protestant traditions do not venerate Mary in this way.

practice_questions.text: 'Catholic Social Teaching is more important than Catholic mission and evangelism.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicitly weighs them; justified conclusion. FOR: Evangelii Gaudium 182–237 places the poor at the heart of the Church's identity; CAFOD's work reaches millions; Matthew 25 suggests serving the poor is serving Christ. AGAINST: Evangelii Gaudium Chapter 5 equally insists every Catholic is a missionary; the Church's primary mandate (Matthew 28:19) is to make disciples; some argue that words (proclamation) and action must be inseparable. Named sources: Evangelii Gaudium; Matthew 25:31–46; Matthew 28:19. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Jesus did and said at the Last Supper in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said 'Take it; this is my body.'
• He took a cup, gave thanks, shared it and said 'This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.'
• He predicted that one of the Twelve would betray him, and that Peter would deny him three times.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Jesus said and did in the Garden of Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jesus told his disciples 'My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death' and asked them to keep watch.
• He prayed: 'Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.'
• He returned three times to find the disciples sleeping rather than keeping watch.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the crucifixion narrative (Mark 15:21-39) shows who Jesus is.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Jesus's final cry — 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' — quotes Psalm 22, a psalm that begins in abandonment but moves toward vindication; this shows him as the suffering servant of the scriptures whose death fulfils God's plan.
• The centurion's confession — 'Surely this man was the Son of God' — is the theological climax of Mark's Gospel; the first human in Mark to call Jesus the Son of God is a Gentile Roman soldier, speaking just after the death, showing that the cross reveals Jesus's identity and that salvation is for all peoples.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the events of Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42) are important for Christians.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for a named source:
• Gethsemane shows Jesus's full humanity — he is 'overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death', demonstrating that the Incarnation was real and that Jesus faced death with genuine fear, which gives Christians comfort when facing their own suffering.
• Gethsemane models submission to God's will — 'not what I will, but what you will' (Mark 14:36) shows perfect obedient trust, which Christians see as the model for prayer and discipleship: bringing one's desires to God but ultimately trusting God's purpose.
The fifth mark requires citing Mark 14:32-42 (or the specific prayer 'Abba, Father... not what I will, but what you will') as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The empty tomb is the most important part of the passion narrative in Mark's Gospel.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Without the empty tomb (Mark 16:1-8), the passion narrative would end in failure. The young man's proclamation 'He has risen!' transforms the cross from defeat into victory. Christianity is founded on the resurrection claim; St Paul later wrote 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17). The empty tomb is the beginning of the disciples' mission.
Against: The Last Supper (Mark 14:12-31) is arguably the heart of the passion narrative — it gives theological meaning to the cross (new covenant, poured out for many) before the death happens. The centurion's confession (Mark 15:39) is the climax of Mark's theology on Jesus's identity. The crucifixion itself, not the empty tomb, is the act of salvation in Christian theology. Mark's Gospel focuses the reader on the cross more than on resurrection appearances.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happened at the tomb on the first day of the week (Mark 16:1-8).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Three women — Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome — came to the tomb to anoint Jesus's body.
• They found the stone rolled away and a young man in white inside who told them 'He has risen! He is not here.'
• The women fled from the tomb trembling and bewildered, and said nothing to anyone because they were afraid.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a Jewish synagogue and their significance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three features with brief significance. Acceptable: Ark (Aron Kodesh) — houses the Torah scrolls and faces Jerusalem, symbolising the direction of prayer; bimah (raised reading platform) — where the Torah is read publicly; yad (pointer) — used to follow Torah text without touching scroll, preserving its sanctity; ner tamid (eternal light) — burns continuously above the Ark (Exodus 27:20-21), symbolising the eternal presence of the Almighty; menorah (seven-branched lampstand) — recalls the Temple in Jerusalem.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Jewish mourning rituals support a family after a death.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: shiva keeps the immediate family at home for seven days while the community visits and brings food, so mourners are never left alone and are freed from ordinary duties at the hardest moment. Way 2: avelut sets a staged return to normal life over 30 days, and the first year for a parent, and yahrzeit brings the family back every year to light a memorial candle and recite Kaddish — grief is given a lasting place instead of being rushed.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Shabbat is important for Jewish families today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way. Way 1: Shabbat is the weekly covenant sign between the Almighty and the Jewish people (Exodus 31:12-18) — observing it strengthens Jewish identity and reminds families of their special relationship with the Almighty; the Friday evening candle lighting and kiddush create a weekly rhythm of sacred time in the home. Way 2: Shabbat is a time for family togetherness, synagogue community and rest from the pressures of work — in a busy modern world it creates dedicated space for what matters most; it models the Creation narrative where even the Almighty rested on the seventh day.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Jewish festivals help Jews to remember the Almighty's actions in history.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Festival 1: Pesach (Passover) commemorates the Exodus from Egypt through the Seder meal, which retells the story of liberation from slavery — this annual re-enactment keeps the formative event of Jewish identity alive for each generation. Festival 2: Shavuot commemorates the giving of the Torah at Sinai — celebrating the moment the Almighty established the covenant relationship with the Jewish people through the Decalogue. 5th mark: ‘Leviticus 23 commands the celebration of these festivals as divinely ordained, ensuring the Jewish community re-enacts its sacred history annually.’

practice_questions.text:
'Shabbat is the most important practice in Judaism.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Shabbat is commanded in the Decalogue (Exodus 20) — one of the Ten Commandments; Exodus 31:12-18 calls it the sign of the covenant for all generations; it is observed every week, giving it greater frequency than any festival; Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described Shabbat as a palace in time; the Talmud treats Shabbat observance as a test case for overall Torah commitment. Arguments against: Yom Kippur is described as the holiest day of the year — its intense focus on atonement and the forgiveness of sins is theologically profound; Pesach commemorates the foundational event of Jewish history (the Exodus); the Shema and Amidah (recited daily) may have a stronger claim on daily Jewish identity than weekly Shabbat; different Jewish communities emphasise different practices. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Exodus 31:12-18 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Bar or Bat Mitzvah and why they are important.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: the young person reads from the Torah scroll in the synagogue for the first time, marking their readiness to fulfil the Mitzvot; the ceremony marks the transition to religious adulthood (13 for boys, 12/13 for girls); the family and community celebrate together, strengthening Jewish identity; the young person delivers a speech ('drasha') on the Torah portion; the Bat Mitzvah is less elaborate in Orthodox communities but equally significant in Reform/Liberal communities.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Hindu festivals and why they are important for Hindus today.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three named festivals with a brief explanation of their significance. Acceptable: Diwali (Festival of Lights, celebrating Rama's return and light over darkness); Holi (festival of colours, celebrating the victory of Prahlad's devotion over evil); Navratri (nine nights honouring the goddess Durga); Dussehra (Rama's victory over Ravana); Ram Navami (Rama's birthday); Janmashtami (Krishna's birthday); Ratha-yatra (chariot festival of Jagannath); Raksha Bandhan (brother-sister bond).

practice_questions.text: Describe the importance of the Ganges as a pilgrimage site for Hindus.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. The Ganges is regarded as the goddess Ganga Mata; bathing in it purifies karma and brings spiritual blessings (1 mark). The Rig Veda 10.75 (Nadi-Stuti) praises the sacred rivers as sources of divine blessing (1 mark). The city of Varanasi on the Ganges is the holiest pilgrimage site — dying there is believed to grant moksha (1 mark). Many Hindus scatter the ashes of the dead in the Ganges to help the atman on its way to moksha (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Hindu pilgrimage is important for Hindus today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason. Reason 1: pilgrimage to sacred rivers (especially the Ganges) purifies karma — bathing in sacred waters is believed to wash away the effects of past actions and bring the atman closer to liberation. Reason 2: visiting pilgrimage sites (Vrindavana, Varanasi) brings the devotee into direct contact with the sacred story of a deity — Vrindavana is where Krishna played as a child, so visiting there deepens bhakti and makes the devotional relationship personally real.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Hindus express care for the environment.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: cow protection (go-raksha) — cows are regarded as sacred symbols of the earth's abundance, connected to ahimsa; many Hindus actively oppose harm to cows and support gaushalas (cow sanctuaries). Way 2: protection of sacred rivers and pilgrimage sites — Hindu organisations such as Friends of Vrindavan restore sacred forests and clean rivers, combining dharmic duty with environmental stewardship. 5th mark: ‘The Rig Veda 10.87 contains a prayer for the protection of creation from harm, underpinning Hindu environmental ethics.’

practice_questions.text:
'Hindu festivals are more important than pilgrimage for strengthening faith.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: festivals are accessible to all Hindus regardless of wealth or mobility — everyone can celebrate Diwali at home; festivals build community identity and transmit religious stories to children; Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28 anchors Diwali in a foundational scriptural prayer; the eight Edexcel-named festivals show the diversity of divine stories celebrated communally. Arguments against: pilgrimage involves physical commitment and sacrifice that deepens devotion — the Rig Veda 10.75 shows the ancient roots of sacred river veneration; bathing in the Ganges is believed to purify karma in a way that festivals do not; visiting Varanasi or Vrindavana places the devotee in direct contact with the deity's sacred story; pilgrimage has been central to Hindu practice for millennia. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least one named source. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Hindu charity work is motivated by religious teachings.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: dana (charitable giving) as a dharmic duty motivated by Bhagavad Gita 3.10-12 (the world is sustained by acts of giving); seva (selfless service) as karma yoga — serving others is serving God; ahimsa motivates care for those who suffer, including animals; promoting women's rights and social inclusion reflects the teaching that all beings are manifestations of Brahman; cow protection organisations embody both ahimsa and care for creation.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that Surah 71 (Nuh) teaches about the Prophet Nuh.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Nuh preached to his people for a very long time, calling them day and night, publicly and privately — showing great perseverance in the face of repeated rejection.
• His people refused to listen, mocking him and blocking their ears — only a small group believed.
• Allah commanded Nuh to build the Ark; after the flood he was called a 'grateful servant' (shakur) in Surah 17:3.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Qur'an says about Ibrahim and Ismail building the Ka'ba (Surah 2:127-129).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Ibrahim and Ismail together raised the foundations of the Ka'ba in Makkah.
• They prayed: 'Our Lord, accept this service from us' — asking Allah to receive their act of worship.
• They prayed for their descendants to be a Muslim community and asked Allah to 'send among them a messenger' — a prayer Muslims see as fulfilled in the Prophet Muhammad.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the story of the Prophet Yusuf (Surah 12) is important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Yusuf's patience through betrayal, slavery and imprisonment shows that trusting Allah even in extreme suffering brings ultimate vindication — his story encourages Muslims to maintain faith and integrity when life is unjust.
• Yusuf's forgiveness of his brothers ('No reproach on you this day; Allah forgives you') models Islamic values of forgiveness and reconciliation, showing that forgiving those who have wronged you is a sign of closeness to Allah.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the story of Ibrahim in the Qur'an shows what it means to submit to Allah.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Ibrahim's destruction of the idols (Surah 21:57-58) shows that submission to Allah requires rejection of all false gods — even when his own community and family worshipped them, he acted on his rational recognition that created objects cannot be divine.
• Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son (Surah 37:99-111) represents the ultimate test of submission — he placed obedience to Allah above even his natural love for his child; the intervention of Allah (providing an animal instead) confirmed that his submission was accepted.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 21:57-58 or Surah 37:109-111 as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The story of Ibrahim is the most important prophet story in the Qur'an.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Ibrahim is described as 'Friend of Allah' (Khalilullah) — a unique honour. He is the ancestor of the Prophet Muhammad through Ismail. He built the Ka'ba — Islam's most sacred site. His willingness to sacrifice his son is commemorated in Id-ul-Adha, one of the two great Muslim festivals. He is the model of rational faith that rejects idolatry.
Against: Surah 12 calls Yusuf's story 'the best of stories' — suggesting it has a unique quality of narrative depth and moral richness. Nuh is described in Surah 17:3 as a 'grateful servant' — a profound model of perseverance. Muhammad is described as the Seal of the Prophets and is the one who received the final, complete revelation — in that sense the most important. Non-religious observers might question the entire concept of prophetic authority, arguing that moral wisdom does not need to be divinely authorised.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which the Prophet Nuh's story is similar to or different from the Bible's account of Noah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point (similarity or difference):
• Both the Qur'an and the Bible describe Nuh/Noah building an ark at God's command to survive a flood — the basic structure of the story is shared.
• In the Qur'an (unlike Genesis), Nuh's own son drowns in the flood because he refuses to believe — this detail is unique to the Qur'anic account.
• Both accounts describe Nuh/Noah as a righteous man chosen by God for his faithfulness in a corrupt generation.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about marriage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: marriage is a sacrament through which God's grace is communicated (1); it is permanent (indissoluble) — 'what God has joined together, let no one separate' (1); it must be open to procreation (1). Other valid Catholic teachings about marriage accepted.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Catholic teaching that sexual relationships should be marital, unitive and procreative.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: marital means sex is only appropriate within marriage (1); unitive means sex strengthens the bond between spouses and deepens their love (1); procreative means sex must remain open to new life and the two dimensions cannot be artificially separated (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the local Catholic parish supports families.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: The Family Group Movement brings families together in small prayer and discussion groups to support each other in faith and family life (2); sacramental preparation classes (e.g. baptism preparation, marriage preparation) help families understand and live the sacraments together (2). Other valid ways accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic teachings about the purpose of the family, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The family exists for procreation — bringing new life into the world and educating children in the faith, which Familiaris Consortio (Pope John Paul II, 1981) calls 'serving life' (2); the family is the domestic church and the first community in which faith is taught and lived, supported by the local parish — Catechism 2226 states that parents are the 'first educators' of their children in faith (2); source credit for naming Familiaris Consortio, CCC 2226, or 'Not Just Good But Beautiful' by Pope Francis (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Catholics are right to say that marriage is only between a man and a woman.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Catholic position: marriage between a man and woman reflects the natural law purpose of sex (procreation), mirrors Christ's relationship with the Church, and is grounded in Catechism 2360-2365 and Familiaris Consortio. Counter: many Protestant churches and the Church of England accept same-sex partnerships; non-religious views argue that committed love is the ethical core, not gender. Evaluate which case is more compelling and why. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: sacrament, procreative, Familiaris Consortio.

practice_questions.text: Explain two divergent Christian views on sexual relationships outside marriage, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen during the Akhand Path.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each. Acceptable: the entire Guru Granth Sahib is read continuously from beginning to end; it takes approximately 48 hours, with readers taking turns in relays; the readers must be initiated Khalsa Sikhs (Rahit Maryada Chapter 7); the congregation attends as much as possible to hear the scripture; the completion (bhog ceremony) is a communal celebration; it is performed at key occasions including births, marriages and gurpurbs.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Sikhs remember or do at Vaisakhi.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Vaisakhi commemorates the founding of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur Sahib in 1699 CE (1 mark). The Gurbilas Patshahi 10 records the account of Guru Gobind Singh calling for volunteers willing to give their heads — the Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward (1 mark). It is celebrated with Akhand Path, kirtan, processions (Nagar Kirtan) and langar; it is also the occasion when many Sikhs undergo Amrit Sanskar (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two features of Amrit Sanskar (Sikh initiation ceremony) and their significance.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: drinking amrit (water and sugar stirred with a sword) prepared by five Khalsa Sikhs while prayers are recited — the initiate drinks and receives amrit on their eyes and hair, symbolising purification and entry into the Khalsa; the sword represents the warrior dimension of Sikh faith. Feature 2: taking the names Singh or Kaur — replacing the initiate's caste surname with a shared Khalsa name; this embodies the Sikh teaching on equality (GGS 349) by abolishing caste distinctions through a common name.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why gurpurbs are important for Sikh communities today.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Reason 1: gurpurbs connect Sikhs to the Gurus' lives and teachings; Guru Nanak's birthday is the most joyful celebration of the faith's founder and his revelation of Ik Onkar (God is One), renewing Sikh identity. Reason 2: Vaisakhi is the annual commemoration of the founding of the Khalsa — it reminds Sikhs of the commitment of the Panj Pyare and inspires new generations to consider Amrit Sanskar; it is also the most common occasion for new initiations. 5th mark: ‘The Gurbilas Patshahi 10 records the founding of the Khalsa at Vaisakhi when Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to give their lives.’

practice_questions.text:
'Amrit Sanskar is the most important Sikh ceremony.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Amrit Sanskar (Rahit Maryada 11 and 13) is the moment of formal entry into the Khalsa — it is the decisive commitment to the full Sikh code of conduct; the Five Ks are visible markers of Sikh identity and faith; Vaisakhi (when many take Amrit Sanskar) commemorates the founding of the Khalsa itself; wearing the Kirpan is a commitment to defending truth at personal risk. Arguments against: Naam Karan links the child's identity to the Guru Granth Sahib from birth — it is the ceremony that begins Sikh life; the Akhand Path (Rahit Maryada Chapter 7) is performed at all major life events and may be seen as more universally important because it applies to both Khalsa and non-Khalsa Sikhs; many devout Sikhs who have not undergone Amrit Sanskar practise Nam Japna, sewa and attend the gurdwara faithfully — the non-Khalsa path is also valid. Secure (7-9): Both sides; Rahit Maryada Chapter 7 or Chapters 11 and 13 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur is significant for Sikhs today.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per significance. Significance 1: Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his life to defend religious freedom — not just Sikh freedom but the right of Kashmiri Hindus to practise their faith; his title 'Hind di Chadar' (Shield of India) shows that Sikh identity involves protecting others, not just oneself; this motivates Sikh commitments to justice and religious tolerance today. Significance 2: his martyrdom shows that faith is worth dying for — refusing to convert under extreme pressure embodies the Sikh teaching that truth and integrity are non-negotiable; his example inspires Khalsa Sikhs who take the Kirpan as a commitment to defend truth.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about marriage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: marriage is a sacrament through which God's grace is communicated (1); it is permanent (indissoluble) — 'what God has joined together, let no one separate' (1); it must be open to procreation (1). Other valid Catholic teachings about marriage accepted.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Catholic teaching about sexual relationships.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: marital means sex is only appropriate within marriage (1); unitive means sex strengthens the bond between spouses and deepens their love (1); procreative means sex must remain open to new life and the two dimensions cannot be artificially separated (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the local Catholic parish supports families.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: The Family Group Movement brings families together in small prayer and discussion groups to support each other in faith and family life (2); sacramental preparation classes (e.g. baptism preparation, marriage preparation) help families understand and live the sacraments together (2). Other valid ways accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic teachings about the purpose of the family, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The family exists for procreation — bringing new life into the world and educating children in the faith, which Familiaris Consortio (Pope John Paul II, 1981) calls 'serving life' (2); the family is the domestic church and the first community in which faith is taught and lived, supported by the local parish — Catechism 2226 states that education in the faith should begin in a child's earliest years and that the parish is a privileged place for the catechesis of children and parents (2); source credit for naming Familiaris Consortio, CCC 2226, or 'Not Just Good, But Beautiful' by Pope Francis (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Catholics are right to say that marriage is only between a man and a woman.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Catholic position: marriage between a man and woman reflects the natural law purpose of sex (procreation), mirrors Christ's relationship with the Church, and is grounded in Catechism 2360-2365 and Familiaris Consortio. Counter: many Protestant churches and the Church of England accept same-sex partnerships; non-religious views argue that committed love is the ethical core, not gender. Evaluate which case is more compelling and why. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why Christians go on pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- To deepen their faith through visiting places associated with Jesus or Christian history.
- To seek healing, believing that sacred sites have spiritual power.
- To do penance — to show contrition for sins through the effort of the journey.
- To feel connected to the events of Christian history (e.g. walking the Via Dolorosa in Jerusalem).
- To build community with other Christians through a shared experience.
Each point must be identifiably separate — do not award a mark for three sentences restating the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why Taize is a significant Christian pilgrimage site.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Taize is a village in Burgundy, France, home to an ecumenical monastic community founded by Brother Roger Schutz in 1940.
- It attracts young Christians from around the world for prayer, meditation, and reconciliation.
- Its worship is characterised by simple, repetitive chants and extended periods of silence.
- It is specifically ecumenical — Catholics, Protestants and Orthodox pray together, making it a symbol of Christian unity.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian Aid puts Christian teaching into practice.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Christian Aid works to end poverty in the world's most vulnerable communities, grounded in Jesus's teaching in Matthew 25:31-46 that serving 'the least of these' is serving Christ himself. By providing emergency relief and long-term development projects, Christian Aid treats those in need as bearers of divine dignity.
- Christian Aid campaigns for justice and systemic change — not only meeting immediate needs but challenging the structural causes of poverty such as unjust trade laws and climate change. This reflects 1 Corinthians 13's description of love as concerned for the welfare of others, not self-seeking.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Easter is the most important festival in the Christian year, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus, which Paul calls the foundation of Christian faith: without the resurrection, faith is 'futile' and Christians are 'still in their sins' (1 Corinthians 15:17). If Jesus did not rise, the cross is simply a tragedy rather than a saving event. Easter is more important than Christmas because it validates the incarnation — the resurrection proves that Jesus was who he claimed to be.
- Easter is the basis of Christian hope for life after death: because Jesus rose, Christians believe they too will rise. The resurrection is not just a historical claim but the reason Christians can face death without despair. 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Christ 'the first-fruits of those who have fallen asleep' — the first of many to be raised.

The 5th mark: name a source — '1 Corinthians 15:12-34', 'Luke 24', or another specific passage. Paraphrase without a named passage does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Pilgrimage is not necessary for Christians today.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support (pilgrimage is not necessary):
- Protestant Christians argue that God is omnipresent: Jesus said 'God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth' (John 4:24). There is no biblical command to visit specific physical places — the New Testament church is built on a relationship with the living Christ, not on sacred geography.
- Money spent on pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela or Jerusalem could be given directly to the poor, which Jesus commanded more explicitly (Matthew 25:31-46). Pilgrimage can be a way of performing visible religious devotion without addressing the deeper ethical demands of the Gospel.
- The Reformation rejected the idea that sacred places confer special spiritual benefits, arguing that this was a form of works-righteousness — trying to earn spiritual credit by visiting the right places rather than trusting in grace alone.

Arguments against (pilgrimage has value):
- Sacred places provide a powerful encounter with the history of faith: visiting Jerusalem and walking the Via Dolorosa gives Christians a physical and emotional connection to the events of Holy Week that transforms understanding of the Passion. Luke 2:41-43 shows Jesus's own family making pilgrimage to Jerusalem each year.
- Taize attracts over 100,000 young Christians annually because its combination of communal prayer, music and ecumenical encounter meets a spiritual need that local parish worship often cannot. The fruit of these pilgrimages — revitalised faith, ecumenical relationships, renewed commitment to justice — is evidence of their value.
- Even for Protestants who reject the idea of inherently sacred places, the discipline of pilgrimage — setting aside time, travelling, meeting other believers — is a powerful spiritual practice consistent with biblical calls to seek God intentionally.

SPaG: 'pilgrimage', 'ecumenism', 'evangelism' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the local church serves its community.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The local church provides practical support for those in need: food banks, street pastors, community cafes and debt counselling services are run by churches across the UK. This is grounded in 1 Peter 5:1-4's call to pastoral care and in Matthew 25:31-46's identification of Jesus with the vulnerable.
- The local church provides a centre of community identity and worship: services, youth groups, parent-and-toddler groups and community events make the church a gathering place for people of all ages. Ecumenical partnerships between denominations ('Churches Together' groups) strengthen this local presence, giving the church a unified voice in the community.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

'The Catholic Church is right to forbid artificial contraception.'
Discuss this statement.

Catholic view: Humanae Vitae (1968, Paul VI) argues that separating unitive and procreative dimensions violates the nature of marriage; natural law supports this. Counter: most Protestant churches accept contraception as responsible family planning; situation ethics (Fletcher, 1966) would say the loving choice should guide each case; Humanists argue reproductive autonomy is a basic right. Evaluate which case is stronger. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which divergent Christian views about divorce and remarriage differ from Catholic teaching, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Many Protestant churches allow divorce and remarriage, arguing that the compassionate response to an irretrievably broken marriage is freedom to begin again rather than lifelong legal commitment to a dead relationship (2); the Catholic Church, by contrast, teaches that CCC 2382-2386 does not permit remarriage after divorce of a valid sacramental marriage, as marriage is a permanent covenant before God (2); source credit for CCC 2382-2386 or Humanae Vitae cited explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Qur'an says about the Prophet Dawud.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Dawud defeated Goliath (Jalut) in battle by Allah's leave, and was given the kingdom and wisdom (Surah 2:249-251).
• Dawud was given the Zabur (Psalms) as a revelation from Allah (Surah 17:55).
• Allah taught Dawud to make armour — his craftsmanship is described as a divine gift.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Surah 19 (Maryam) says about the annunciation and birth of Isa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jibril appeared to Maryam and announced that Allah would give her a pure son — she asked how this was possible since no man had touched her.
• Jibril replied 'Your Lord says it is easy for Me; We will make him a sign to the people.'
• When Maryam presented the newborn Isa to her people, he spoke from the cradle, declaring himself a servant and prophet of Allah.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Islamic teaching about Isa in Surah 4:157-158 differs from the Christian understanding.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• In Christianity, Jesus died on the cross and rose from the dead — the crucifixion is the central act of salvation. In Islam, Surah 4:157-158 states Isa was not killed or crucified; Allah raised him before death occurred — crucifixion is therefore not the basis of salvation in Islam.
• Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God who died to atone for human sin. In Islam, Isa is a great prophet and servant of Allah — born of a virgin, performing miracles — but not divine; his death (avoided by raising) is not understood as an atoning sacrifice.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Maryam is an important figure in Islam.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Maryam is the only woman named in the Qur'an and has an entire surah (Surah 19) named after her — this unique honour places her among the greatest figures in Islamic tradition, held up as a model of purity, faith and total submission to Allah's will.
• Maryam's experience of the annunciation and miraculous birth of Isa demonstrates Allah's unlimited creative power — 'Your Lord says it is easy for Me' (Surah 19) — and affirms that Allah can act outside natural processes when he chooses; this is a sign for believers.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 19 (Maryam) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Muslims should not try to convert other people to Islam in modern Britain.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support (of the statement): Humanists argue that everyone has the right to their own beliefs and that attempting to convert others shows disrespect for religious freedom. In a pluralistic society, imposing one religion's truth claims risks division and harm. Non-Muslims may find attempts at conversion unwelcome or pressurising. Secular law in Britain protects freedom of religion.
Against: The Qur'an commands Muhammad to 'warn your nearest kin' (Surah 26:213-217) — a divine obligation that Muslims believe applies to all believers. Sharing one's faith is not the same as compulsion; Surah 2:256 states 'there is no compulsion in religion.' Da'wah (invitation) based on gentle persuasion and good example is the Islamic model, not force. Isa foretold Muhammad (Surah 61:6), showing that prophets always invited others — it is part of the prophetic tradition. Many Muslims see their commitment to social justice and ethical living as a form of witness that respects others' freedom.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Qur'an says about the life and mission of the Prophet Isa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Isa was born miraculously of the virgin Maryam without a human father, by Allah's direct command.
• Isa performed miracles — healing the blind and leper, and raising the dead — as signs of his prophetic authority.
• Isa foretold the coming of a final messenger called Ahmad (Muhammad) in Surah 61:6.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of the call of the disciples as described in Mark's Gospel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Jesus called fishermen (Simon, Andrew, James, John) beside the Sea of Galilee and they left their nets immediately to follow him (Mark 1:14-20).
• Jesus called Levi, a tax collector, with the same two words 'Follow me', and Levi got up immediately (Mark 2:13-17).
• Jesus sent the Twelve out 'two by two', instructing them to take nothing for the journey — no bread, bag or money — showing radical dependence and trust (Mark 6:7-13).

practice_questions.text: Outline three things that happen in Mark's account of the rich man's encounter with Jesus (Mark 10:17-31).
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• A man asked what he must do to inherit eternal life; Jesus told him he lacked one thing — to sell everything, give to the poor, and follow him.
• The man went away sad because he had great wealth.
• Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the Kingdom of God.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Peter's denial (Mark 14:66-72) is important for understanding discipleship.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Peter's denial shows that discipleship can fail even in those who seemed most committed — this warns Christians that discipleship requires ongoing reliance on God's grace rather than human willpower or self-confidence.
• The specific mention of Peter in Mark 16:7 ('tell the disciples and Peter') suggests that failure is not the end — Jesus offers restoration to those who have failed, giving hope to disciples who struggle.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the life of either Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Oscar Romero or Mother Teresa reflects the demands of discipleship in Mark's Gospel.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for a named source. Example using Bonhoeffer:
• Bonhoeffer's resistance to the Nazi regime reflects Mark 8:34 — 'deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me' — he quite literally risked and gave his life for his faith, demonstrating that discipleship may require sacrifice of personal safety.
• His book The Cost of Discipleship argued against 'cheap grace' — a Christianity without cost — mirroring Jesus's teaching in Mark 10:45 that the Son of Man 'came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.'
The fifth mark requires citing Mark 8:34 or Mark 10:45 as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The women in Mark's Gospel are better examples of discipleship than the male disciples.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Women are present at the crucifixion (Mark 15:40-47) when the male disciples have fled. Women are first at the tomb (Mark 16:1-8) and first to hear the resurrection proclamation. The anonymous woman who anointed Jesus (Mark 14:3-9) is praised by Jesus: 'wherever the gospel is preached... what she has done will also be told.' The Greek/Syrophoenician woman (Mark 7:25-30) persists despite apparent rejection and is praised for her faith.
Against: The male disciples were called first (Mark 1:14-20) and were sent on mission (Mark 6:7-13). Peter's confession 'You are the Messiah' (Mark 8:27-33) is a moment of genuine insight. Peter's failure (denial) is followed by restoration (Mark 16:7 — 'tell the disciples and Peter'). Judas's betrayal is the disciples' worst failure, not a representative picture. Mark's Gospel is more interested in showing the challenge of discipleship for all than in ranking disciples by gender.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Parable of the Sower (Mark 4:1-20) teaches about discipleship.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• The seed on the path represents those who hear the word but Satan immediately takes it away — some people do not respond at all to Jesus's call.
• The seed on rocky ground represents those who receive the word with joy but fall away when trouble or persecution comes — discipleship requires perseverance through difficulty.
• The seed in good soil represents those who hear the word, accept it and produce a large crop — true discipleship bears fruit in a changed, productive life.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Catholic view: Humanae Vitae (1968, Paul VI) argues that separating unitive and procreative dimensions violates the nature of marriage; natural law supports this. Counter: most Protestant churches accept contraception as responsible family planning; situation ethics (Fletcher, 1966) would say the loving choice should guide each case; Humanists argue reproductive autonomy is a basic right. Evaluate which case is stronger. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: Humanae Vitae, contraception, procreative.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which divergent Christian views about divorce and remarriage differ from Catholic teaching, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Many Protestant churches allow divorce and remarriage, arguing that the compassionate response to an irretrievably broken marriage is freedom to begin again rather than lifelong legal commitment to a dead relationship (2); the Catholic Church, by contrast, teaches that CCC 2382-2386 does not permit remarriage after divorce of a valid sacramental marriage, as marriage is a permanent covenant before God (2); source credit for CCC 2382-2386 or Humanae Vitae cited explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Christians use the Bible in their daily lives.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Reading the Bible during personal devotion (private worship).
- Hearing the Bible read in church services — liturgical churches follow a lectionary ensuring all Scripture is covered over time.
- Using the Bible as a source of guidance when making ethical decisions.
- Reading the Bible for comfort and strength in times of difficulty.
- Using the Bible in study groups, Bible classes or Sunday School.
Each point must be identifiably separate.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways the Cross is significant as a Christian symbol.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- The Cross is the primary symbol of Christianity, representing the crucifixion of Jesus and the means of salvation.
- Ephesians 2:10-19 describes Christ reconciling people to God through the cross, 'destroying the barrier, the dividing wall of hostility.'
- Different denominations use the symbol differently: Catholic and Orthodox churches typically display a crucifix (cross with the figure of Christ); many Protestant churches display an empty cross, symbolising the resurrection.
- The Cross appears in churches, on jewellery, in art and in corporate logos as a universal marker of Christian identity.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians interpret the authority of the Bible in different ways.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The Bible was written by many human authors over centuries in different literary genres (poetry, law, history, prophecy, letters), which makes uniform literal interpretation problematic. A poem like Psalm 103 cannot be read the same way as a historical account in Acts; understanding the genre and context shapes interpretation. This leads many Christians to hold an 'inspired' rather than a strictly literal view of biblical authority.
- Christians disagree about the relationship between the Bible, Church Tradition and individual conscience. Protestant Christians, following sola scriptura, hold that the Bible alone is the final authority; Catholic teaching (Dei Verbum) places Scripture and Tradition alongside each other, with the Magisterium as the authentic interpreter. These different starting points produce different ways of weighing what the Bible says against what the Church has always taught.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why art, music or drama is important in Christian worship, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Visual art (paintings, icons, sculpture) helps Christians focus on the realities of faith that words alone cannot express: an icon of Christ or a painting of the Crucifixion draws the worshipper into contemplation of divine truths. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2502 says sacred art 'evokes and glorifies, in faith and adoration, the transcendent mystery of God.'
- Music deepens worship by engaging the emotions and memory: Gregorian Chant has been used in Catholic and monastic worship for over a thousand years, creating an atmosphere of prayer and reverence. Contemporary music by Graham Kendrick and Casting Crowns makes faith accessible to new generations, expressing belief in forms culturally relevant to today's worshippers.

The 5th mark: name a specific source — 'Catechism of the Catholic Church 2502', 'Ephesians 2:10-19 (the Cross)', 'Musicum Sacrum (1967 Vatican document on sacred music)', or a named artist/work. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The role of women in the Church should be equal to that of men in all Christian denominations.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- Romans 16:1-16 shows women in significant leadership roles in the early Church: Phoebe is called a diakonos (deacon), Priscilla is a co-worker in the Gospel, and Junia is described as 'outstanding among the apostles.' If women held these roles in the New Testament Church, the Church today should reflect this equality.
- The Church of England ordained women as priests in 1994 and as bishops from 2015; the Methodist Church has had women ministers since 1974. These denominations argue that the Gospel breaks down gender hierarchies ('neither male nor female... all one in Christ Jesus') and that the Kingdom of God is characterised by equality.
- Limiting women's leadership roles restricts the exercise of the gifts the Holy Spirit gives to all believers (1 Corinthians 12). The Body of Christ needs all its members functioning to capacity.

Arguments against:
- The Roman Catholic Church teaches that its inability to ordain women to the priesthood is a definitive teaching: Christ chose twelve male apostles and the Church has no authority to change this. This is not presented as a cultural preference but a theological conviction about the nature of the priesthood.
- 1 Corinthians 14:33-40 has been interpreted by many evangelical and Catholic Christians as indicating that authoritative teaching in the assembly is a male role. Some argue this reflects a created-order principle that transcends cultural context.
- Some Christians argue that equal dignity does not require identical roles: men and women can have complementary roles of equal value. The Catholic and Orthodox traditions affirm women as essential to the life of the Church while reserving the ordained priesthood to men.

SPaG: 'denomination', 'conscience', 'Reformation', 'Filioque', 'ordination' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which CS Lewis's writing expresses Christian belief.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950) uses allegory to communicate the Christian doctrine of atonement and resurrection: Aslan (representing Christ) allows himself to be killed by the White Witch (representing evil and sin) and returns to life, breaking the 'deep magic from the dawn of time.' Readers engage with the themes of sacrifice, redemption and resurrection through a fantasy narrative rather than a theological treatise — making the ideas accessible to children and adults unfamiliar with Christian doctrine.
- The Great Divorce (1945) explores the nature of heaven and hell through an allegorical journey, presenting heaven as fully real and earth as merely 'the shadow-lands.' Lewis argues that people who reject heaven do so by clinging to petty selfishness — they choose themselves over God. This expresses the Christian teaching that hell is ultimately self-chosen separation from God rather than external punishment.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]
